The rabbit flees; the tiger must be stroked backward before it can be caught—so Linji laughed. It is no hindrance to flaunting one’s idle spirit. From the beginning, no one has recognized this story.
When Luzu saw someone, he merely sat facing the wall. His compassion truly does not lie in many words. Amidst ten thousand divergences and a thousand differences, one should appreciate them.
Like lightning rolling and stars racing from the crown of the head, waves surge and billows crash beneath the feet. To kill or to give life depends on the moment.
The tips of arrows meet; adding mud upon the earth, he administers blows and shouts. With his staff, he casually stirs the great void.
East, west, south, north—there is no room for deliberation; eighty-four thousand beings are all liberated. Is it merely this?
Behold further how it illuminates heaven and mirrors the earth.
Next, regarding the rhyme of the Heart Hermitage Song by Venerable Gaṇeśvara (Gan-yun):
Elder Huanzhu said, "Gā! Gā! A single 'Heart Hermitage' cannot be established; one knows only that opening the mouth results in error.
How was it back then with Mazu? The bright moon in the heavens cannot be compared to it; the snow is cold upon the courtyard.
Seeking it within the state, one does not call it a hermitage, nor does one call it a thing. Nameless and characterless, it encompasses all; the vastness of the three realms—how could it have an end?
Stretching out both legs to sleep in bliss, there is no rival. On all four sides there is no obstruction; how narrow can the great void be?
Let them drag the curtain down before them as they please; neither sage nor ordinary person is established therein.
If you say that the myriad phenomena are of one accord, I say it is merely a chance occurrence resulting in obstruction. When the mirror is free of dust, there is no need to wipe it further;
the mind is the hermitage, and the hermitage is the mind. What limitation can there be between the south of heaven and the north of earth?
Sending off Chan Master Zhong to visit Jingshan, where many request a verse:
[I go] up to Jingshan; Chan Master Zhong shall likewise head toward that place. At the foot of Mount Jiyun, the four willow switches are picked up and used to strike down the dragon king’s nose.
That Master Qin was deluded by this as if it were trivial; how could it depend on Mazu’s perfection?
In the intervals between [meditative] states, I now dwell in leisure and am likewise mute. In years to come, there will surely be no one to scold me.
I see off the Chan practitioner Ying for Mount Lu.
Ying came to Danchu; two summers passed as if they were a single day. Although my four elements are slightly at ease, a single thought is quite real.
"Listen attentively to my words! Exert yourself with focused diligence! Abandon the near to pursue the far; cast aside the crooked to establish the straight.
For this reason, within your daily life, there is only loss and no gain. As for the wondrous Dharma-gates of the Three Mysteries, when have they ever established boundaries?"
The Buddhas and Patriarchs originally share the same path; the vast void leaves no trace or mark. It is like Mahesvara, who keeps one eye wide open.

To cease delusion, you must know for yourself; to seek the Truth, it becomes increasingly difficult to find. On this journey to Mount Lu, I have visited and studied under all the excellent spiritual friends.
The myriad realms suddenly open into emptiness; the divine mechanism emerges in transcendent clarity. When you return again on another day, how limitless will your laughter be as you lift your brows?
To send off Zen practitioner Huī on his journey to Zhejiang:

The Three Essentials and Three Mysteries. Reflecting the earth and illuminating heaven, authority and reality, illumination and function, the eyes and their movement, the wondrous embrace and the simultaneous inclusion.
Pervading throughout the sands of the world, each and every part is distinguished by host and guest; emerging and submerging with the full capacity of the mechanism, all is without obstruction.
Abiding, it is not like [anything]; being like [something], it does not abide. Having eaten the clear water and white rice of Zhejiang, one knows shame and remorse.
With the third eye of Mahesvara opened wide at the crown of the head, one can surely be expected to pick up the spoon and set down the chopsticks.
To the Chan Master Ning:
It would be better for you to cut out your tongue than to violate the imperial taboo. A single phrase cuts off the flow;

when a tall man enters the water, he turns his body about upon a ten-thousand-fathom cliff—ten thousand layers and a hundred circuits, impossible to avoid. He picks up the lantern and strikes the pillar. The child of Kunlun—his eyebrows!
The table stands upright, piercing through the pearls within the mani-treasury; boundless pure light illuminates heaven and earth.
I bid farewell to Chan-man Pu as he travels south to Mount Wu.
The mountain is high, the lake is shallow. The mountain being high, it is difficult to climb; the water being shallow, it is easy to see. I intend to take up my long fishing pole.
Fishing for the giant turtle: do not let the fishing line be lost. The waters are vast and boundless; it cannot be found.
He kicks over the Eight-Character Stele atop the peak. His mother-born eyes are as bright as lightning.
Following the rhyme of Master Xugu, I send off Attendant Jue:

from sleeve to sleeve, the golden mallet is wielded. From of old, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have transmitted and upheld this; whether one is ordinary or holy is of no concern—struck once with the hammer, all is shattered without remainder.
Picked up at random, nothing is rejected; every thing and every situation is laid bare. One must know that it extends ten thousand miles.
Divine light shines forth with brilliant splendor wherever it reaches; how could it depend on mere abundance or harmony?

To deliberately seek out flaws and blow upon the razor-sharp blade—unless one cuts it off dead at once, one will only see more errors being passed along. Deep within the channel there is naturally water;
the void has originally no interior or exterior. Look at the Five-Tufted Peak: dust and weeds rise together from the bottom of the well. *Maṇidhāri*.
"Śrī. This is the profound essence of our house, the Dharma verses proclaimed by the realized masters of the Zen school.

It is not like the poems of novice students who practice prosody to mock the wind and sing of the moon, being merely constrained by rhyme. Rather, it is simply that sounds and voices are used to provide a rough semblance of likeness.
"Nearby" (*jin*) is simply used as a rhyme. However, as for the refined pronunciation of those from Zhejiang, when words flow from the mouth, they naturally harmonize;
they would certainly not use the character *máo* (hair) as a rhyme with the character *hé* (harmony).
Only among the venerable masters of Fujian is it common to use characters such as *gāo*, *dāo*, *máo*, and *háo* within the "Gē" and "Gō" rhymes. Master Xugū, moreover...
A person from Wuzhou. Although Wuzhou is located in Zhejiang, its local accent is extremely harsh and difficult to understand.
When "mao" (毛) is now used as a rhyme between "he" (和) and "e" (訛), it is simply due to that regional dialect.

Furthermore, whenever I observe the accents in Fujian, the high tones are pronounced like "ge" (歌), "dao" (刀), "duo" (多), "mao" (毛), "mo" (摩), "hao" (豪), and "he" (和). For example, in the current [reading of] Dongshan Kong...
The *gāthās* and *ślokas* of the Chan masters were widely circulated in the world, and their general character can be seen therein.

For instance, in the *Verses on the Four Modes of Deportment*, the character "to" (到) is used as a rhyme with "sitting" (坐箇); the character "to do" (做) is used as a rhyme with "staying" (住) and "vinegar" (醋);
and the character "way" (道) is used as a rhyme with "seat" (座). In such cases, they are merely slightly similar. Furthermore, as for ordinary people...
It is said: the tails of snakes, tigers, and the like are called "weiba" (尾巴). This is the character "ba" (巴) from the phrase "Bashé" (巴蛇), written in its standard form;

it is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*), with the phonetic transcription *bāngjiāqiè*. However, in the verse for seeing off his elder brother Liàn to Yúnmén, Dōngshān uses the rhyme within the departing tone (*qùshēng*) category, writing the character as "wěibǎ" (尾靶).
This is pronounced in the departing tone, with the phonetic transcription *bìjiàqiè*. Furthermore, "bǎ" (靶) refers to the leather thong of a bridle, used by the charioteer.

This is a matter of handling things as they arise. This is precisely how the great masters of the tradition wield the brush according to the occasion, merely to demonstrate the true Dharma-eye to others;

who cares what anyone else thinks? As for the younger generation today, they have largely abandoned the practice of Zen meditation and desire only to study words and phrases—how can they even be compared to those [ancient masters]?
Fuzang the Abbot departs for Jingshan; from Jiangzhe, he travels far away and returns again.
Eating by the water and lodging in the wind, his spirit is vast and leisurely. You must know that entering the forest does not stir a blade of grass;
let the ancient path be covered in green moss. When answering the monk’s inquiry about characters, he simply speaks of them; he does not speak of this Way now.
It is like ashes. Do you not see? "At the ten-thousand-fathom peak, the Dragon Gate opens; the overnight guests do not come, and the fish expose their gills.
This is also a regulated verse form that has been transformed into an ancient-style poem.
I see you off, Attendant Yishi, as you travel to the eminent sites of Zhejiang;

within the ultimate truth lies the meaning of reality. Among the eighty-four thousand gates of worldly affliction, a single word has not yet come forth—how I am ashamed of my own dullness and silence.
The Yellow River flows in nine bends from Mount Kunlun; the pearl possesses luster so the stream is beautiful, and the jade is without flaw so the stone remains warm.
Having traversed from the head of Wu to the tail of Chu, one must distinguish between clarity and turbidity before one's eyes. Casting down the rhinoceros fan, one casually cuts off heaven and earth.
The four sevens and two threes are all at a loss; hundreds of thousands of Buddhas vie with one another to rush forward.
This single poem is also distinct. The first six lines have a sound resembling that of Li Bai’s poetry; the final six lines do not.
Furthermore, from the fourth line through the fifth and sixth, they closely resemble it.
Presented to Wu Shishan at Zhuo’an:

In the practice of the Way, body and mind must be true and real. Reaching this point, there is no distinction between Confucianism and Buddhism. Indeed, when one thought is suddenly forgotten, one becomes foremost in both the mundane and the transcendent worlds.
The daily activities of all sentient beings are already fully perfected; as for choosing or rejecting, acting or withdrawing—there is none.
It is indeed certain. For the precious treasury of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), seek no other. From this, the nature-ground (*dharmatā-bhūmi*) emerges, perfectly luminous.
The lay devotee Wu Shishan of Fanyang possessed a resolve as firm and solid as metal and stone; together with his wife, Lady Chen, he gave rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).

He vowed to escape the realm of worldly toil and afflictions (*kleśa*). Amidst the nets of greed and anger that entangle the world, and the dense thickets of self and others that are deep and impenetrable—Shishan...
Having grasped the sword of wisdom, the Chen family likewise cultivated the power of compassion and patience. Wealth and possessions were cast aside and entrusted to their descendants;

for the light of time passes like a dream, in the space of a mere instant. To seek the truth and still the thoughts, the principle naturally becomes clear; sever worldly attachments and banish the traces of human presence.
Trimming the weeds and clearing away the shadows, he constructs a thatched hut. Transcending the sages and surpassing the ordinary, he leaves behind mind and consciousness.

The Southern Mountains rise steeply in azure green; the jewel groves and flowering trees stretch straight on together. The practitioner does not depart from the ground of the mind; even when departing, how could he ever be entangled by thorns?
Reciting sutras, reciting the Buddha’s name, and further reciting the Dharma—there is neither lack nor excess, neither gain nor loss. Simply proceed from here.
In this life, one naturally attains the realization of the pāramitās.
To the Chief Librarian and the Rector Heng:
Since time immemorial, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have left no trace; the people of Jambudvīpa do not recognize them. Yesterday, the Daoist [Master] came from Mount Lu himself.
Come. My home is north of the Stone Bridge in Tiantai. I say this path is now desolate; yet, undaunted by blistered feet, you have come from afar to exchange our wares.
By the river, the ripples are as black as lacquer; three men wish to buy, but who can resist? Since I took up residence here, my wrists have grown weak.
Who understands how to wield the ancient knife and ruler? For now, sit and let us brew tea together behind the house, while listening to the iron chime.
Knocking on the Chamber of Ambrosia.
Following the rhyme of Master Dongyu, I send this verse for Chief Seat Huī.

In the past, when Muzhou came to Shaoyang, he entered the gate and let out a breath that overwhelmed all quarters; at the moment of his encounter, a single pressure left his feet [hanging in the air].
Broken. To this day, he bears the pain and cries out to the azure heavens. The Head Seat Dongyang brandishes his golden staff, awakening humans and devas with a thunderous crash.
His pungency surpasses that of Old Muzhou; he does not sweep away the words, but sweeps away the traces.
The spring breeze is lush and profuse upon the idle branches, yet there is the "Wish-Fulfilling Sword" to prune them away. Brought from afar, it enters my chamber; it fears not the waters.
The mountains of Bing are vast and distant; soaring through the void for ten thousand *li*, one watches the Peng bird take flight. Who listens to the murmuring of the swallow in the beam?
It is precisely now that the five-petaled flower blooms; only then can one truly shake the earth and startle heaven.
Next, following the rhyme of Layman Bidaoyao:
"Darmatara did not understand Chan; the Master did not know how to read. Each was ignorant of the other; why then did you establish a 'founder's teaching'?"

Far-reaching, beyond the void kalpas; vast and all-pervasive, perfectly complete. From the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, across this land and the Western Heavens—it is as if one were merely extending and contracting an arm, or opening and closing a hand into a fist.
One must realize that within this Great Transformation lies the root of the ceaseless turmoil of birth and death.
No-mind is itself the Way; to accord with principle is fundamentally not "Chan. I hope you will manifest a refined brilliance; do not merely guard this lump of deluded flesh.
Send it to the Elder Chan Master of the Western Hall by the Yangtze River;
he has a mouth that explains for himself. Even his speaking would cause one’s tongue to knot up—how much more so when one has personally ascended the *svastika* [the mark of the Buddha].
In the hall, sitting grandly by the window, he divides the wind and moon. How pitiable is this little Śākyamuni; how clumsy are his skills!

As soon as the Indian monk crosses the threshold, one should have cut him down right there before his face. To wait further for him to display supernatural powers is nothing more than using a tethering stake for a donkey.
Why not stand atop the peak and observe the deployment of means? When word and deed correspond, every step naturally transcends. Atop the peak...
White waves surge from the void; beneath the well, dust and weeds shroud the sun. When the time comes, one suddenly arrives at Lake Dàn-jīn;
though one exhausts the depths, not a single drop remains. Having bid farewell, where do you wish to go? Return to seek the old mountains. Within the city of Yánzhōu, there is a clamor and din;
the *dharmakāya* is startled awake, with no place to be found.
The Abbot Chì was sent by the Master to build a stupa. Where has he gone?
Deep autumn, the trees have shed their leaves, and the frosty wind rises. When will he return? Next year, in the second month, the peach blossoms will bloom.
Casting sand and scattering earth, he presents his bewildered sack; under the blue sky and bright sun, clouds and thunder arise. The Patriarch.
A single sandal—sparsely worn, it remains on Mount Xiong for a thousand years. The Old Man of the Eastern Mountain has coarse strength;
barefoot, he carries it upon his shoulder halfway along the path. Yangqi’s one hat, with its seven holes and eight rips, no one knows.
Deeply hidden at Vulture Peak for ages, he brought it forth with both hands, yet the Master would not accept it. The sacred bones of the former teacher remain even now; I wish to return.
Add yellow earth to cover it. Have you not seen how Shushan was greatly incensed when building his stupa? He paid the craftsmen only three or two coins each.

If you go to various quarters to test the waters, do not let you tread upon and shatter the Dragon’s Den.
Sent to the Chan Practitioner Shang of Guangnan:
Three before and three after. A bright pearl from the sea emerges from Guangnan;
presented at the gate of a wise teacher for inspection, a single wheel of frosty moon shines upon the cold pond.
Next, two verses on the rhyme of Shanglan and Zhutian:
The fame of his reputation has already been widely heard. In the city of Hongzhou, he opens the great gate wide. Look at the place where the corners meet and the patterns interlace;
A hundred turns and a thousand layers resolve themselves spontaneously.

Shame and remorse arise together with the conditions of the eastern waters; with the strength of one’s own arm, one reveals the true void. Does the Old Master Liang of the Western Mountains know this?
As spring ends, flying flowers are red everywhere.
Seeing off a monk who pays homage to the Patriarchs:
the gateways of the ancestral masters are overgrown with weeds. Who will clear the path for him? It is said that when his hands are level with his chest, he has understood;
I know not on what day he shall return again.

Master Shou shows that the lifespan of this body will not last many days; as the ancient worthies once said, it passes like a horse through a crevice. You have traveled on foot again to seek mountains and waters;
as for your own field, what is it truly like?
Seeing off a monk who had traveled to Shushan to pay homage to the Patriarchs, I asked:

"Regarding the 'Short Abbot' (Aoluo), whose stature and voice were so remarkable—how many truly know his extraordinary place among the masses? It is said that the wooden snake has now come back to life;
one must observe the moment the command is issued upon entering the gate."
Inscription for the "Embracing the Green" Studio The windows and doors of this studio on all four sides stand wide open. Layered distant mountains send forth their greenness.
Even the white clouds seem to understand human intent; They depart as rain and drizzle, never to return.

Listening with the head at the mountain stream, one returns the hearing until it reaches the hearing-mind; picking up the handle of the ladle, one probes the shallow and the deep. From beginning to end, not a single sound is allowed to enter the ear;
thin mist enshrouds the banks, a profound and silent blue.
Carrying forth a fine verse in the style of Master Xueyan, I have brought it here to Dajin. I know for certain that you are Jizang’s former incarnation;
from the *bīḍa* leaves, a fragrant breeze arises, scattering as a uniform springtime throughout the world.
Following the rhyme of Master Guyun, I see it clearly, yet it is not yet true.
The patriarch’s core essence knows no partiality. At dawn, the sun halts upon the cold river;
how many can truly show their heads beyond the heavens?
Seeing Off Master Chu at the Banks of the Chu River:
The waters flow eastward by the walls of the Chu city; Be careful not to wander aimlessly seeking elsewhere.
Last night, a single orb of moonlight from the depths of the waves Floated up, limpid and stainless, its cool radiance shimmering.

Sending Star-Master up to the heavens, where the stars are clearly and distinctly arrayed; yet in the human world, ten thousand matters compete in their confusion. Though the patch-robed monk has eyes, he cannot see them;
he mistakes them for the gateway to the Buddha’s myriad practices.
Seeing off a Zen practitioner bound for Mount Jing:
"The ceaseless throng are all still halfway there. I am ashamed that this Zen practitioner has gone to Mount Jing and retrieved a single pearl from the Dragon King;
he now comes to present it to me, the old monk, for my inspection."
Yuan Shuying’s style name was Jingchu (Abiding in Stillness).

He sought the practice of stillness within the midst of clamor; yet while he observed that worldly fame and profit were irrelevant to him, he had not yet realized that all phenomena are like illusions.
Thus, his desire to escape the toil of the mundane world remains a great difficulty.
Chetui-na seeks the ancient Buddha’s compassion down to the present day; from beginning to end, it is the grandmotherly heart. Dangu never followed after him;
with a hot shout and a wrathful fist, he sought to restrain you.

Seeing off Master Shou as he departs to visit his teacher, and then departing again to travel among the various masters to visit his teacher once more—such was the bearing of people of old. Did not Guling merely know how to rub one’s back?
With a single blow, he clearly seized the tiger’s whiskers.
Master Jùn served as the abbot at Mount Jing;
he has traversed the gates and courtyards of all masters of knowledge. The waters of Lake Dàn are shallow and difficult for a boat to moor;
atop Mount Língxiāo one watches the sun rise, while below lies the abyss of ten-thousand-fathom dragons.
Seeing off Zen Practitioner Hui on his journey of transformation:
the great task is accomplished in an instant. Do not grieve over the hardships of the road;
three thousand *li* away you shall meet a true friend, who can cause the five-petaled flower to bloom beneath the brush.
When Yuan showed his new precepts to Yangshan, Yangshan saw that there was indeed no "Yuan" remaining in his breast; he should have been instructed to study under Xiaoshijia.
Compared to this, Great Chan has no skill at all—though the rattan staff may be broken, one cannot surpass it.
Two Poems Sent to the Elder Lan Jing at Mount Ding:
Traveling three thousand *li*, I have arrived at the banks of the Dan River. Among old friends, our sentiments are deep; there is no one else to part with.
Quickly you must cast wide the net that covers the heavens, And take care to ensnare the white phoenix and the qilin.
I spent an entire night contemplating it at Mount Ding; yet how difficult would it be to seek out Beidu? It is better to simply use Xuansha’s method:
sealing it with white paper is just as effective.

I tell the envoy from Liangzhou that the grapes here grow without trellises; The new vines atop my roof were personally transplanted by my own hand. Beside the window, I have no desire to prop up high frames;
I shall simply wait for the autumn wind to bring forth their fruit.
Setting up shelves before the eaves is a labor spent in vain; moreover, there is the breeze from the palace corner that brings coolness.
Last night, looking at the new leaves by the western wall, the *reiju* flowers slantingly entwine within the grassy hollows.
To see a master while traveling for study, one must possess the eye for travel; in the battle of Dharma, one must be versed in the tactics of that battle.
Hold firm the black staff used for testing the waters; do not follow Old Zhao to Zhuyou.

As I see Master Yuanchang off for Jiangxi to pay homage to the Patriarchs, Buddha hands Buddha without a word; from patriarch to patriarch, they have mistakenly pointed out tracks. Eighty-four men roll along like wheels;
until now, they remain in a mess within the weeds.
A monk is sent up Mount Jing:
one clear phrase is as straight as a hook. Once the fragrant bait is cast, it strikes the head of the giant turtle.
How much better it would be to cast down the long pole and sit watching as the clouds are gathered in a single net.
Sending off Master Xinyuan as he enters Zhejiang:
A single staff, amidst mist and rain, departs from West Sichuan. With right mindfulness perfected and the power of the Way firm, the gateway of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is as deep as the sea;
there is no need to hesitate—buy another boat for the Zhejiang River.
Spontaneous Verses upon Hearing the Cuckoo:

The soul of the Shu-魄 (soul of the cuckoo) on the mountain peak fades away in secret; Ancient trees cast deep shadows over the village beyond the city walls. A single cry from across the shore is even more piercing;
Last year in the land of Wu, it was never heard.
Lamenting for Master Hengxi, Five Poems On this day, why is my soul alone so desolate?
My old friend has passed away, a thousand miles away, separated by life and death.
I know not who, outside the lacquered black wooden shrine, Will accompany you through the cremation as you leave the temple gate.
We parted at the foot of the tower in Wujiang at the third watch; he passed away before Mount Jinzifeng one day later. Since then, my feelings have been so deep and my grief so profound;
yet, look at it from this perspective, what harm does it do to the Way?
Illusion perishes and illusion arises; a single bubble. True Suchness and its apparent divergences differ by a thousand paths. Before the skull lies the grass of Bodhi;
after the fire, the old sprouts shall surely grow once more.
Re-reading the letter sent by you in days past, it is entirely composed of instructions on the supreme principle. Having finished reading, I have no worry that I shall not respond;
such a friend as you is rarely seen.
I weep before the wind, offering this cup of tea; life and death truly bring no grief for you. It is simply because the trees of the Jetavana have few leaves left;
once they flutter down, it is autumn once more.
Seeing Chan Master Man off for Jinling:
The Chan master takes his leave of me for Jinling; With moonlit oars and wind-filled sails, he sets out on his journey. I am told that lately the spring waters have filled the rivers;
Even at night, the tides still crash against the Stone City walls.
To whom can these verses on sending off the monk be explained? This mind is known only by the Old Barbarian.
When the season of deep autumn returns once more, I shall drive the awl deep behind your head for you.
I sent Li Langzhong three medicinal prescriptions;
the journey by which they arrived was exceedingly arduous. On this day, how could they be bestowed upon others? Fortunately, he is a master physician for the world who heals the state;
it is fitting that these be transmitted so that the weary people may live.
A twin-headed lotus with joined calyxes and linked stems emerges from the water; one stalk, one fruit, and one flower pedestal.
I recall having seen it once within the Eight Virtues Pond, specially blooming for the Golden Immortal’s two feet.
In the same rhyme, I show this to my junior attendant, Venerable Hu:

Old as I am, my sentiments have passed through the years; Among those before my eyes, there are few who are truly diligent. The discourse on the broken sand-pot carries the weight of ten thousand catties;
To lift it up—how can one’s wrist-strength suffice?
Ten Poems by Tiantang, with Preface (Nine Poems Now Collected).
My friend, the Head Seat Duangiang, was staying in the mountains. When I returned from the fields, he came out to meet me and immediately said:
I have been in Wu for several years now. I have felt a sense of deficiency because the two poems on Lingyan and Huqiu Mountains remained unfinished.

Recently, amidst the deep waters and cold mountains of Baiyun, I attained a profound resonance with the subtlety of those two landscapes; thus, I have readily undertaken the search [for inspiration] and have now completed them.
I hope you will provide me with some editorial guidance. I replied: "Poetry is not my forte. I am currently dedicated to making the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs my own responsibility;
I lament the decline of the Dharma community and grieve that later students have failed to flourish. I strive to practice that which I have not yet mastered."

One must be earnest regarding that which one cannot yet achieve. Only when each person has individually realized the natural splendor of their own fundamental ground, and has opened the eyes of humanity and the heavens to continue the lineage together, will there still not have been even a hair’s breadth of benefit—how then would there be leisure for the affairs of prosody?
Recently, while staying in this small courtyard, I have lacked the strength to delegate tasks; whether matters were great or small, I necessarily attended to them myself.
Even when going to the fields to collect rents, I encountered the deceitful and sly among the commoners, who claimed fertile fields as their own while assigning poor ones to me.

In every situation and circumstance, these were all matters pertaining to the three karmas of greed, anger, and delusion. Although I attempted to guide and restrain them by means of the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, it was entirely ineffective. Thus, the reeds...
By the willows at the edge, the herons are chilled and the gulls are cold; the waters are solemn and the frost is clear; the wind has ceased and the moon is white.
This is sufficient to provide for my joy in the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna. Unconsciously, these thoughts took form in speech, and as I sang them, they became ten verses.
I have titled them "Songs from the Fields," for they truly cannot be compared to conventional poetry. I venture to present this record for your inspection.
The hardships of a daily life are not many; the sentiments of dwelling in the mountains should naturally wear away.
Without cause, one goes once more into the forest, passing through thatched huts and straw-roofed sheds quite by chance.
The wind is swift, the frost cold, and the rain has just cleared. A few strokes from a soft oar emerge from the solitary city.
Beyond the western horizon where no one dwells, the moon shines again through the branches of the trees.
A north wind blows across Lake Yangcheng; intending to moor my boat, whom shall I ask?
By the reed-banked shore beneath a withered tree, leaning against the precarious mast, I sit through the hour of Qi.
Eating by water and lodging in the wind, I have arrived at the village home. Meeting you, there is no word—just a single cup of tea.
I truly feel regret that my preaching of the Dharma has not benefited sentient beings; when will the roots of the Way sprout?
The grain has already been harvested from the threshing floor but not yet ground into flour; how could the farmers know the old man who dwells among the mountains?
With a cup of village wine, let us offer a casual toast; let us forget all formalities in our mutual humility.
I send these words to my companions on the mountain paths to know: The old man by the river has taken up his plow.
To the south and north of the village, where people dwell in sorrow, It is precisely the time when the west wind brings the rain.
The vegetables and wheat are lush green, yet the rice is already gone; the farmers have still not returned their rents.
If one were to judge the high and low by mere measures of grain, one would find that people’s speech before others has become coarse.
In warmth, kindness, and propriety, I am surpassed by the gold; in cleverness and eloquence, I do not equal him.
I win only the profit of a few pecks before my eyes, yet I know not what shall become of me after death.
Once you have rowed your oars amidst ten thousand surging waves, you shall likewise stir the ripples within a single hoofprint. Let neither the young nor the old be surprised;
for how can this total mechanism of appearing and disappearing be grasped?
The late master Gulin and Master Duanjiang both inherited the lineage of Hengchuan, yet their respective accomplishments differed significantly.
The preface to the *Tianzhong Ou* likely serves as a critique of this. What has been collected here is likewise intended precisely not to include that *Ou*.
By reviewing its sequence three times, it may serve as a mirror for those who study the Buddhas and Patriarchs; one simply cannot cast it aside.

Yet, as for his innate talent for cutting through the river of words and the excellence of his compositions, which have become "minced meat and roasted meat" for the public and made him a renowned figure of the age—such a thing is rare indeed.
As for his ability, he was able to manifest that [ultimate reality] within this [phenomenal world].
If one brings this forth and proclaims it, what more could there be? Yet as for its being negated, I do not know why.
Six Verses in Mixed Prose:
The spiritual blade, a precious sword, is held in the hand; the chestnut thorn and golden circle are girded at the waist; three children embrace a flower.
Drum! Do not come to block me as I leap before you.

The karmic conditions of Buddhas and Patriarchs have become a fallen heap of words. The ocean of karma for sentient beings is a sea of suffering, shifting between heat and cold. Without a single speck of dust remaining, I pick it up once more;
the mountains and rivers of the great earth proclaim it themselves.
Having become the great Dharma beam of the Tathāgata, one must exert effort as soon as the *huatou* is raised. Even a dog lacks Buddha-nature, yet it still possesses [the capacity for life];
when the cart moves, it is the ox that moves it.
The numinous light of Prajñā penetrates everywhere; within a smile and a conversation, hundreds of thousands of samādhis unfold. Deshan did not understand the final phrase;
when the white staff was brandished, his artistry was exhausted.
Only just set foot within the thicket of thorns; yet in the sandalwood forest, the fragrance has not been heard. The colt tramples the four quarters of the world to death;
of the eighty-four [patriarchs], none have a path to travel.
The sound still lingers upon the stringless zither; the leaves are even fresher upon the shadowless branch. The Gate of Non-dual Dharma has been fully opened;
Vimalakīrti’s illness was likewise just so.

Living in the mountains as I grow old, dwelling among the peaks naturally stirs my feelings; the springs and rocks within my cottage are pure throughout the four seasons. How could one who plants his staff fear poverty for lack of land?
In discerning things, I only loathe a mirror that is not clear. The jade pitcher is filled to the brim with shards of ice; the silver bowl is piled high with snow.
Yingying. The black staff does not stir from the corner of the meditation seat; at times, a wind arises, echoing through the myriad valleys.

Sent to Administrative Assistant Jia, whose reputation alone is preeminent in the court. His merit in supporting and upholding the gates of the Teaching is complete. Where the Way is about to prevail, form and name [manifest].
Extinction. When the Sangha is honored, ritual and music flourish. A single pool of water is crystal clear to its very bottom; a name of high renown is like the moon suspended in the sky.
It causes the cold valley to return to the springtime—this all resides within the impartial bellows of the Dao.

On the Occasion of Events by the Lake The season of the three winters is utterly desolate and cold; How much more so when one dwells amidst the waters and rocks by the lake. The ice has frozen solid, leaving my moored boat at the broken bridge;
Willows wither on the precarious bank as I gaze upon the distant mountains. How swift the noble horses return upon their path! How quickly the numinous birds pass before my eyes!
No more returning. This is truly the finest scenery at dusk: the full moon shines round upon the branches of the aged plum tree.
In this same rhyme, I present this to Lin Xuezheng, "Beginner":
When all affairs are in turmoil, what can one rely upon? How could the mountains be steep, and how could the waters be level? In leisure, the white days pass away; my feelings incline toward this.

Excellent. Entering the azure clouds in a dream, my thoughts grow ever lighter. The words established at the banks of the Zhuyi and Si rivers are truly worthy of admiration; the instructions bestowed upon Vulture Peak are likewise clear.
Cease judging the high and low by means of gain and loss; a single mat by the lakes and mountains is sufficient for its own purity.
Self-Description of My Hermitage Life:
In my old age, finding leisure is truly appropriate. Sitting motionless upon my rush mat, I am simply like a fool.

As soon as worldly concerns and attachment to the self arise, one is immediately bound by fame and constrained by position. The path to my door is overgrown with weeds and rarely visited; in the earthen stove, the coals glow early in the spring.
First, eliminate [the distractions]. Next year, at fifty, add one more layer. Do not look back too often at the horse passing through the crevice.
In this rhyme, I send these lines to Master Dongyu:
"Brother Dongyu’s style is profound; truly it transcends all worldly sounds. It shall cause even the heavenly Māras to fall away."

The gallbladder (dharma-nature) is not only able to overturn the minds of scholars; it maintains this state of ordinary reality, so do not engage in speculative calculation. Do not attempt to grasp its functional mechanisms, for they cannot be shouldered.
Where there are seven penetrations and eight apertures in every direction, even the keenest hawk’s eye or copper-colored vision cannot easily find them.

Though the number of masters of the Dongshan lineage, such as the Venerable Dongqiu of Damei, was not small, he alone left behind this old Chan monk of Meiling. Picking it up, he immediately uses the line at the tip of the fishing pole;

where it falls, the shuttle on the loom does not pause. Disliking the Buddha, he refuses to act for its sake—this must surely be his own prerogative. Borrowing function to clarify position, it is fitting that...
Return it! When one utters a single taboo name right before one's face, who can touch it? One sings "Li-ra" by oneself before the wind.

For a wondrous Chan practitioner seeking wondrous, perfect, and transcendental awakening, this is precisely the moment; how much more so for a child of our own house who has leaped over the hearth! In the East and in the West, there is no Buddha.

The Patriarch: Who else is it that travels south and north? The falcon strikes with its swift wings, soaring beyond the clouds; The dragon plays with the divine pearl, leaping upon the shore of the sea.
Last night, the spring breeze shook the trees in the courtyard; At Shaolin, two or three branches of blossoms have burst forth.
The Venerable Yì (Yi Weina) transformed incense and candles, chanting *geya* and *gāthā* with wondrous tones. For ninety days he cultivated and realized the Way, manifesting profound merit.

The Buddhas of the ten directions proclaimed it in unison, and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans gathered solemnly before him. Not only did he thoroughly eliminate subtle delusions, but he directly led others to investigate the very source.
The coming mind. With incense, flowers, lamps, candles, and ritual ornaments, the donor himself provided the gold.

Next, Zhuang the Head Seat followed the rhyme and power [of the verse], exploring the vast ocean and traversing the land of Shenzhou. Like a drifting duckweed with a solitary trace, he floated according to his nature; only after experiencing many cycles of heat and cold did he finally awaken.
Dawn! Who would have known that the *púliù* trees would again be startled by autumn? To withdraw the self in every way is a skillful means; to let all affairs follow conditions is to attain freedom.
Fortunately, Guizong’s mattock still remains; for whom shall the function of "slaying the snake" be requited?
Having met my old friend amidst the mountains, the secretary Jiao Gong, I joyfully send word of my whereabouts to the riverbank. A lifetime has already seen through all vanity;
throughout the three periods of time, no cause for affliction arises. Beyond the gate, the clear waves leave no path to pass; atop the peak, the azure well flows of its own accord.
Dust arises. How could this practice depend on grasping the essential framework? The master of Ying merely boasts of his axe for carving the nose.
When sending off the monk Jiaqiao, he once departed from Zhejiang; today, as he contemplates returning, he has traveled through the region of Wu three times.
Carrying it, he lowers the oar and turns his body; there is one mechanism missing. The boat passes over Lake Dongting and Qingcao; birds carry heavy barriers as falling flowers fly.
The streams, mountains, clouds, and moon are all alike; by deliberating upon the realm of phenomena, one long ago entered the subtle.
The Venerable Zhenjue Pǔshǒu came to visit;
he is the foremost person in the Hall of True Awakening. Having traveled far to speak with such earnest devotion beneath the pines, I reflect that my old indolence has rendered me useless.
Yet your beloved son’s spiritual edge enters the divine with wondrous skill. A sword dripping blood above the Brahma Heaven; an arrow piercing the red sun in its eye.
A medium-quality sinew. A thistle-stalk cudgel that incites people to eat. The venerable elder speaks now of Old Chen;
Elder Yi is old and lacks the heart to continue this lineage.
He departs to seek the compassionate countenances of the various patriarchs, letting the mud beneath his feet be as it may.
A single foot-measure: who can measure how many layers of human paths there are? The iron-and-stone heart and mind remain ultimately unchanging;
the atmosphere of mountain forests is inherently the same [as one's own nature]. When departing, why indulge in frequent idle talk? One’s own radiance penetrates everywhere.
Seeing off a monk heading south for the Zhejiang examinations, I ask:
what is so urgent about his travels? Having stayed at Pó Lake, he now goes to Qiántáng. He will surely seek out a true teacher at Língxiāo;

there is no need to hide his person within the Northern Dipper. At the bottom of the well, the dust and weeds are just beginning to sprout; atop the mountain, the clouds and trees are already flourishing.
Azure and vast. With the eye of the crown of the head alive, one distinguishes the black from the white; this is no ordinary fellow, Meng Bārláng.

When the two lay devotees, Chen and Song, built the Huanglian Bridge—spanning the void, cutting across the ravine, and framing a flying rainbow—their single-minded sincerity was as unyielding as iron and stone. This was not merely for the sake of relieving the ailments of the people of Su.

To traverse this path, one must simply manifest one's own true style. The conditions of the vows made over three lifetimes remain; the living road through mountains and rivers for a thousand miles is open.
From here, the yellow swallowwort forms a magnificent vista; observe those who tread upon the morning frost.
Sending off Chan Master Jizang to Lingyin: "Return it to its author; he knows.
The crown of his head is vast and clear, revealing the towering majesty. How could he fear three thousand li when traveling freely?
Face-to-face, the foremost mechanism cannot be deceived. He need not worry that his monkey-arms are too short for probing the waters; yet in forging friendships, he often fears the crane’s cry.
Flocking together like birds, on Vulture Peak a single handle gives rise to a bundle of reeds; suddenly grasping it, one settles right and wrong.

Understand that Manager Xu’s poetry and ritual have been passed down from antiquity to the present; this mind can truly accord with the Mind of Heaven. Resounding throughout the region south of the Zhe River is his illustrious reputation.
Respectfully submitted. The atmosphere of Jiangdong is truly profound; the Dharma indeed relies upon you as its bulwark. You are truly fit to serve in the halls of statecraft and glory.
I know for certain that you will not forget our pact from three lifetimes past; we shall sit together beneath the green shade, gazing at one another at this lakeside temple.
Entrusted to the Great Master of Mt.
Mui, he sits upon his great seat facing the courtyard, an ancient Buddha-field. Space has no mouth, yet it proclaims itself. Held crosswise or used upside down, paths are divided;

as the thread goes and the silk comes, one measures the long and the short. If you cannot manifest it through display, you must manifest it; before you have even begun to deliberate, [it is already here].
Deliberation. If we meet and merely laugh "he-he," the transgression is too great for a dwarf to bear.
Following the original rhyme to see off the guest-master Li:
When meeting, why must one raise the tea bowl? The protocols of the monastic community have already been observed; moreover, the dust of worldly attachments has been entirely swept away.
All is exhausted. What mental preoccupations or questions of origin remain? At the river’s edge the setting sun finds those seeking lodging; outside the gate, the western wind drops leaves in autumn.
When mountains and rivers are turned back into one's own self, there is no harm in placing a head atop a head.

In the same rhyme, I send off Attendant Zhong: As soon as one attains the state of no-mind, one should rest. Excessive words make it increasingly difficult to harmonize with the Way. A single thought spanning ten thousand years is like the moon in a clear pool;

Ignorance throughout kalpas is like a monkey facing away from a mirror. When a wild goose flies across the vast sky, its shadow still lingers; When a dragon roars in a withered tree, it is precisely [the moment of awakening].
Encountering autumn, master and disciple meet; they clearly realize this profound principle. Seated, they cut off heaven and earth at the very pinnacle.
Following the rhyme of General Xu for his birthday:
"Two days before this auspicious date in the heavens, a portion of the human realm nurtures the emergence of the worthy and sage. Amidst the fragrance of lotus flowers, the carriage arrives.
Horses and oxen; within the voices of women, pipes and strings are played. The aged cypress defies the frost, lush and verdant; the peach of immortality bears fruit, perfectly round.
Three thousand years of events remain much the same; soon we shall see the writ of the fungus descend from beyond the sun.

In the same rhyme as Director Xu: His towering reputation resounds throughout the scholarly community; for a thousand ages, the heart of the Sage Confucius remains unblemished. By nature, his disposition is able to transcend the mundane;

through family tradition, he upholds loyalty and filial piety, reviving the fading echoes of antiquity. Beneath the fine trees before his hall, he lingers in tranquil seclusion; by the flowing spring at the foot of the cave, he finds his companion.
Shouyin: Tomorrow the mountains and rivers shall truly share in the auspicious omen; your colorful robes will surely broaden the heart of your northern hall.
[In the same rhyme, I send off Master Yizang as he visits his parents:
The gate and courtyard of Shaoshi are cold as ashes; how could mere mastery of speech encompass it? Even if one were to sit upon the meditation seat...
Broken. It would be better to consult the teachings so that one’s own eye opens. When the compassionate mother is in the northern hall, she should wear the colorful robes;
in the palace of the Dharma King, moss ought to grow. Have you ever known how not to tread upon either of these two paths? Master Chanji has returned for a second birth.

Entrusting oneself to T'ien-ch'ang at the Snowy Peak, the patched-robed disciples vied to pursue the fragrance of his Way and virtue. They did not shrink from the journey to seek T'ien-ch'ang, seeking but a single word to escape the nest and coop, so as to avoid falling into the extremes of annihilation and permanence for many lifetimes.
As flakes of ice fill the streets in the midst of intense heat, the Iron Ox emerges from its neck to await [the seeker].
A fresh coolness. Meeting with a smile atop a thousand peaks, the tradition of the Yaoyao Gate has flourished for long.
Following the rhyme to send off Attendant Jin on his visit to the Master, two verses:
The decree has been in effect over the Wu and Yue regions for years; looking at it today, one fears it may not yet be so. Without traversing the journey, he still acts as...
Understood. When one wishes to separate mud from water, they add a whip; when spreading out a single robe to sell, there is originally no price. To copy out a paper gown is not Chan.
I have heard it said that this master has nothing to do, yet he extensively opens up dry land to plant golden lotuses.
Body and life unconfined, I wander as I please; for half my life I have traveled on foot to visit famous mountains. Only when the single blow lands upon my ribs do I know the pain;
within the three responses to my voice, I have already penetrated the barrier. Whether it be the essential and the profound, or the clear and the distinct;
whether it be toil and labor, or ease and leisure—when teacher and disciple meet, there is no need to ask anything at all. It is simply fitting to look at one another and break into a smile.

I send these words to Chen Caolu, who has mastered several portions of the primordial *xiāntiān* numerology. How could I dare to discuss one's poverty or success before others? It is not for the sake of flattery or seeking contemporary fame;
I simply wish to let my reputation be heard by all. When the fish leaped through the Dragon Gate, the thunder shook of its own accord; when the sun rises over the Cang Sea, its waters follow.
No trace remains. This old monk takes up his staff and brings it forth; hung upon the head of the bed, it has its own root.
To the Layman Heqzhou:
When Master Pang [Jiayuan] of yore took Ma Zu as his teacher, today you, Heqzhou, pay homage to Gautama. There is no need to allow Han Shan and Shide to come and compete.
Tongue. For now, engage in dialogue with Fenggan; distinguish them, yet never give rise to a single thought. At times, allow the holy and the ordinary to be fellow practitioners.
As for the Seven Reversals and Eight Inversions of Tao Pengze—even knitting his brows, he was still unacquainted with them.

The Tripitaka Master departs for the capital, overturning the ocean of the canon and emerging from the lake of the frontier. It is precisely the season when the autumn wind first causes the leaves to fall. Steadily he sails his iron boat across the vast expanse;
with a staff of bramble slung across his shoulder, he ascends the imperial capital. Upon his bed at night, the cries of crickets ring out piercingly; from the Milky Way, wild geese fly down.
The shadow is solitary; fundamentally, no form or trace remains. Zhaozhou hangs a gourd on the eastern wall.
Sending off Head Seat Hua to travel to Wu, his investigation of the *huatou* is as vast as the void.
The foremost figure in the hall of the lake temple—how could a raging conflagration allow for mosquitoes or gnats?

Mooring here, one must be like an elephant king to cut through the current. Reflecting thus, I recall the empty courtyard of Shaoshi at evening; now I come to behold the spring of the imperial gardens among men.
Having perfected the ancestral pivot of the seventeen hundred [patriarchs], I carry my staff over Mount Lu and enter the clouds of Wu.
Seeing off a monk for Tianmu:
the waters of Lake Dan are shallow and boats find it difficult to moor; Mount Tianmu is high and not easy to ascend. When the oars turn, the steps must shift.
What has the Buddha ever awakened to? What can the Patriarch accomplish? One should possess the eye of Maheśvara upon the crown of the head; in a dark room, one ought to light a lamp.
Lamp of the World: Having crossed the iron threshold of the western peak, he returns to gallop upon the edges of ice.

He has sent off the head seat Haedong In, extinguishing the lineage and extinguishing the gate of Master Myeong. The ancestral家风 (family style) of our patriarchs has been swept away and no longer exists; accustomed to traversing the ocean’s edge, he treats the snow with ease.

Waves. Having once ascended the immortal peaks and gazed upon Kunlun, I have come afar to this lake temple with even deeper feeling. Entering the celestial palace in a dream, my Way grows ever more honored.
Not a single word shall I spare—it is like an iron stake—to ensure that others take up the burden and carry it down to their descendants.
This was none other than the former Abbot Jōchi, the distinguished successor of Bin-in. Formerly his sobriquet was Metsushū, but upon returning to court, he changed it himself.
He was also a close friend of mine; observing his personal etiquette, he appeared to be a man of profound sincerity and integrity.
Now, I know not where he has gone—could this be the nobleman’s fondness for seclusion?
A Gift for the Water-Moon Temple’s Collection of Translated Scriptures in the Great Capital:
In the midst of the water-moon light, a dharma-hall is established; The scrolls of the *Mahāsāhasrapramardana-sūtra* are to be spread and proclaimed together.

Before a single speck of dust is analyzed, one must achieve perfection; To renew the Tripitaka, we rely on your leadership. Though not yet written beneath the brush, the brilliance of the text is already revealed; Within the scroll, the name is first inscribed.
Fragrant incense—not only to extensively plant the merit of *dāna*, but further to pray that the sun and moon of the Yao-heaven may endure long.
As the Abbot Lin enters the Meng Hall at Tiger Hill, he has turned the entire Tripitaka in a single breath;
even when monks gaze upon it, their eyes wither. Zhongfeng is truly a gateway of the mouth.
Narrow! At Mount Hu, it does not hinder sparse teeth. Let go, and there are a thousand phrases throughout heaven and earth; gather them in, and the Buddhas and Patriarchs are utterly nothing.
Turn yourself around and look at the tips of the hundred grasses; let the great earth be like a furnace of flames.
Eight Verses on the Zen Practitioner’s Hwadu:
The old man Shao Yang’s hwadu is profound beyond measure; He understood that the Dharma-body emits two kinds of light.
When the sun stands at its zenith atop Mount Sumeru, Each and every thing is seen as it truly is, in its ordinary state.
A single phrase, once heard, revives the ancestral wind: the southern mountain burns charcoal, the northern mountain glows red.
If one can discern the subtlety within this, even gold dust may be picked up and placed in one’s eyes.
In the Great Way, when has there ever been right or wrong? With eyes born of the triangle, one distinguishes dragon from snake. Before every door is a torch;
when asked about the Buddha, the answer is three catties of hemp.
The fine scenery before the window is truly profound and secluded: A verdant pond with red lotuses opens under the dew. Directly beneath, one clearly realizes the seal of the mind-ground;
It encompasses the entire dharma-realm, utterly free from even a speck of dust.
Tearing asunder the blue seas, he leaps across the whale; plucking out the pearl from beneath the jaw of the black dragon.
With its vast, divine radiance containing the precious moon, when brought forth, it is truly enough to terrify the foolish.
Muzhou visited Huangbo in the past; Linji sought out Dalong in his day. They were equals, both climbing the same immortal cassia tree;
who would say that the wind is not the same across a thousand li?
Throughout my life, I have eaten coarse food and worn rough clothing; my speech does not startle the world, yet it naturally penetrates the subtle.
What follows is a long discourse to be continued on another day: a hairless hawk soars close to the heavens.
Casting it here and tossing it there was not in vain; when our Buddha first took birth, he pointed his finger toward heaven.
I had thought that Yantou’s prediction was empty, yet indeed Deqiao reached his goal in only three years.
Entrusting this to the Venerable Wanshou Wushou:
karmic offenses as vast as mountains are instantly emptied. One seeks their point of origin, yet no trace remains. The cataracts that clouded the flowers no longer sprout buds;
upon the branches of the iron tree, the sun rises red over the sea.

Taking leave of the donor T'ien-p'ing regarding the incense and lamps of this one quarter: the white clouds are deep, and layer upon layer of cliff-dwellings are encroached upon by mossy rings. Ten years of ascents and descents have occurred in a single day;
I cannot bear to express my gratitude for the hearts of all the donors.
Seeing off Attendant Wu to Zhejiang:
Awakening is the same as when one has not yet awakened; the samādhi of the patch-robed monk must be deeply understood. Eat your meal this morning and you are full this morning;
before dawn arrives, the belly is hungry again.
The matters within the three responses have already been resolved; one simply does not know upon whose family the bright moon will fall. Is this old monk’s heart so earnest?
Outside the gate, the spring breeze brings blossoms everywhere.

The gateways of the Right-of-Zhejiang are as deep as the sea; If you have not yet clarified the ground of the mind, you must seek it through inquiry. Upon your return, you shall surely receive a great blow;
Sixty strokes of the willow branch are not easily restrained.
Qian Luan and Wu Yuanku seek the art of carving and engraving lotus flowers with refined mastery; ten thousand stalks of *udumbara* emerge from the water in crimson bloom.
Even if the void of dharmas serves as the Buddha’s seat, one must still sit upright within the jeweled pedestal.
To send off Zen practitioner Xing:

A single thought correctly aroused is perfect and complete; there is no need for tedious further questioning of the way. At the crossroads of the street, the Buddhas of the three periods of time are present;
the original ground of the mind is utterly clear.

Sengyi, you Zen practitioner, have recognized Old Man Qici of Changting; you may now set out on your travels to叩 (knock at) the ancestral winds. I, Xiujue, am old and have nothing more to entrust to you:
outside my gate, the autumn light rests within the clusters of chrysanthemums.
Mao De-yong seeks the Way in the *Zhongyong*;
do not seek it falsely. Simply let the mind-ground rest at once. The hundreds of thousands of Buddhas have all realized this profoundly;
there is no need for further effortful cultivation over many lifetimes.
I, the clumsy Chan practitioner, ask Master Xing:
"How does your clumsiness compare to mine? My clumsiness is great; having grown old without virtue, I have ultimately wasted my time. When the ninety-day period is complete, I must return;
will you join me before the Master with palms joined?"
The great excellence of their material clearly manifests the rise of my school; Linji once planted cypress trees on Mount Qiao.
Not only do they provide shade and coolness to cover the world, but they require the labor of building pillars and beams a thousand feet high.
Presented to the Chan Master Bi: The Lotus Sutra Written in Blood.
From the tips of the ten fingers of Bi Chan, more than sixty thousand mani-jewels were shed. How wonderful! This is the inexhaustible treasury for all sentient beings;
Sitting and watching, the fragrant dew drips upon the lotus flowers.
Seeing off Attendant Ya to visit his parents:
Their kindness is deep and must not be forgotten. At this cool autumn season, he departs for Qiantang. When the letter arrives, do not disdain the black paper robe;
leave it by your bedside to release its radiance.
I bid farewell to the Great Master of the Western Tubo:

beneath his feet lie tens of thousands of layers of clouds and mountains. Having traveled extensively through the south, north, west, and east, he finds that the gateways of the Patriarchs are as deep as the sea, yet they are all right here in the midst of the bustling marketplace of red dust.
Originally there is neither self nor person; why toil so hard over the quest for the ford? What was written upon the white paper has become a second [copy].
Stepping out the door, the flowers and willows are once again renewed.
A foreign monk sets out to pay homage at Potalaka;
having crossed the shifting sands, he traverses the Yellow River. Again he heads south to worship at Potalaka; beneath his feet, the waves and billows stretch for tens of thousands of fathoms.
When Avalokiteśvara beholds him, what does he do?
Layer upon layer of mountains, one after another. At midnight, the golden sun shines once through them all. How many times have white clouds failed to pass?
Yet they leave the dark path open for people to traverse.
The source and flow of this ancient stream have come directly from the beginning of the kalpa; it pours forth as a wild torrent, a barrier that cannot be turned back.
Even if one were to stare with wide-open eyes to reach its very bottom, even Xuefeng would find his mouth unable to open.
Two Verses on the Separate Source:
Trickling forth, it does not join the common currents; Chasing the waves and following the ripples, it is vast and boundless. Yet in the end, the deep blue ocean lacks even a single drop;
Where in the great trichiliocosm does it not flow toward its source?
One knows not from where this single drop comes; it flows into the vast ocean amidst heaps of white waves. To say it is Caoxi is still not enough;
for now, let people guess its depth and shallowness.
If there is no self and no spirit, what more need be said? Is it not before the vast kalpas of Vīradhvaja? To the very end, not even a thousand sages were taught to eat;
only then do we know that the hidden intent lies right there with him.
Boundless and vast, it encompasses the worlds of the sands; this is his entire body. Ten billion Mount Merus are but a single speck of dust. Looking east, it is south;
looking west, it is north. Upon the crow’s head, the golden wheel turns.
The Chan practitioner inscribed the *Lotus Sūtra* in golden characters to provide for the reception of guests at Mount Ling;
he sought seven scrolls of the *Lotus Sūtra*, totaling sixty thousand words. The assembly on Mount Ling remains as it was; gold naturally has its own price.
The treasure place is clearly before one’s eyes.
Seeing off the Venerable Píng:萍梗相逢盡半途 (萍梗相逢盡半途).
When arriving home, do not say there is nothing to say. The names of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas are but idle words;
it is precisely here that one should deliver a single blow before others.
Seeing the five hundred oxen of Tiantai all at once as a monk departs for Putuo and Yandang,
Jñānagupta still remains at the Great Dragon Pool; further employing the supernatural power of the Great Being,
he wanders across the sea with a *khakkhara* staff slung over his shoulder.
Listening to the spring, I sit in night-meditation until the deep of the night; the stream flowing around the house utters wondrous sounds. These eighty-four thousand sounds are not mere verses;
they are intended solely to cause one to realize the original mind.
The two *zangzhuchi* (treasury masters), Huai and Xuan, have returned to their old mountain;
surely they had made a pact. The crane has left the treetop, yet remains silent.
I know not how many days’ journey across the sea it will take after its flight, compared to Master Xian’s own travels.
The crane departed without a sound. When compared with Master Xian’s verse, was it perhaps a spontaneous omen? Or was it truly the profound discernment of Master Cheng?
For what reason did Master Xian immediately become a long-term attendant at Xuedou? As for the practitioner Xian, he later appeared in the world [as a teacher].
He succeeded another master. He was rebuked by the Mountain Granny in front of Xuedou, who said:
"Xuedou shook out his bowels to preach Chan for you; how can you be so ungrateful and ingrate? This refers to that very point. Master Xuan was like this.
Master Xuan was a native of Quanzhou, named Chengxuan, with the style name Wuyan. This was because the Master resided at Huqiu under Yuanzhao Lingyuan.
During his time at Zutang Monastery, he served under Master Guo (莒公) with diligent devotion, inquiring after and receiving instruction on the Way of the Dharma.

When he requested further guidance regarding Xuedou’s *Capping Phrases on Ancient Cases*, the Master selected one hundred cases to re-explain for him; these were later compiled and circulated in the world.
Furthermore, he composed a preface to the collection himself, stating: "I had the honor of serving as his attendant, inquiring and seeking instruction day and night. Truly, my mind was awakened."
As for this person, he proclaimed his succession to the world after [his predecessor], yet he also inherited the legacy of another.

Although he was not subject to the terrifying verbal abuse from the mountain front that befell Master Xuán, he nonetheless incurred even greater censure from the "clear waters" (the scholarly community). He previously resided at Yángfén Zífú Monastery.
Later, he resided at Jiangxin and Nengren on Mount Yandang. His Dharma path did not flourish, and he experienced constant adversity;
yet this was simply his destiny—what else could it have been?
In the diagram for recollecting the Buddha, there is one circle and one Amitābha; within that circle, the Buddhas are most numerous.
At the clear dawn, gazing upon the lotus pond, countless dewdrops adorn the fresh lotus leaves.

At the Tiger Hill Assembly, the Head Seat was invited to preach the Dharma at the Heavenly Palace. In my dream, it was exactly as in ordinary times. From the tip of his tongue, ten thousand apertures roared;
the four seats were struck with such awe that a cold wind arose. The four lines of verse are fundamentally non-existent; what use is the emptiness of the hundred negations? The wild goat...
The horn has not yet been hung; upon the great earth, there is no trace of movement. The precious sword is just now emerging from its scabbard—who would dare face its blade?
This eight-sided clarity is exactly like this: the blazing sun shines upon the peak of Mount Sumeru.

The Master of the Repository, Jixian, has never heard such a summary of the essential phrases. On one hand, they summon each other with a bond of profound sincerity; for every ox received, a horse is returned.
It does not hinder one from picking up the broken sand-pot.

This was precisely when he was staying with the Brahmacārin. At that time, while [the Master] was presiding over the *bǐfú* (dharma-brush) at Qingliang, the members of the Bao-ning community all arrived.

Upon his return, they reported to the Master all matters concerning the raising of the essential principles, the question-and-answer sessions, and so forth. The following day, they were treated to a meal of noodles and wished to invite the Master;
however, anticipating that he would certainly not come, they consulted with the Abbot, Chan Master Dongling, saying, "If we could obtain your..."
At first, he simply thought that because the Abbot had invited him, he would certainly attend. Ling gave his assent; however, he immediately revealed the intent of his plot.
The Master said, "I was precisely waiting for him to ask about the essential principles [of our school], yet you have instead come to summon me first?
He then took ten *chǔ* (paper currency) notes and composed this gāthā, which he burned as an offering. Attendant Yuan carried it to the Abbot, who then recited the gāthā.

Afterwards, he again inscribed: "One *mian* (measure of flour), ten cash in silver notes, sent as a modest contribution. Respectfully submitted by [Name] to his old friend, the Curator Zhu Xian. The character *mian* (flour) is used here for *mian* (one).
The radical on the side, the character for "wheat" (*mai*), has been omitted; it is used solely for its phonetic sound.

Furthermore, the word "one" (*yi*) in the phrase "one face" (*yi mian*) contains two meanings: first, it refers to "one"; second, it refers to the "face" (*mian*). Thus, it carries a double significance. One means... [text ends].
"Offering noodles to summon one another" means, first of all, to summon one another exclusively by means of signs.
"Come, come! Son of Zen, sing 'Come, come!

The stone field and thatched hut have their doors always open. The divine light is never obscured; it is the intention of ten thousand ages. Before the sharp point of the pivot has even been touched—"
The Three Mysteries are shattered. Come, come! Before the sound, vast and surging, it roars like a spring thunderclap.

Who can cover their ears? They cannot hear it in time. For my sake, call back the Golden Ox and awaken him! Son of the Bodhisattva, son of the Bodhisattva! Everyone eats their food in much the same way;
yet how few know how to vomit forth their very liver and entrails? To benefit things and benefit people, there is truly a profound purpose. Come, come, come! You must come even further!
Before the temple of the ancient Buddha, cease all deliberation and conjecture. The golden rooster knows how to hold the grain; the jade horse ascends Mount Kunlun.
Sudhana’s southern pilgrimage through a hundred cities is profound and vast; the multi-storied pavilions stretch far along the cloud-path.
This was also precisely for the sake of those who act as Brahmā-sages.

Śākyamuni renounced the rank of a golden-wheel-turning monarch to enter the realm of worldly toil; the three realms were vast and desolate, and the path grew ever more remote. For forty-nine years, he practiced...
All is exhausted; Vulture Peak still pierces the heavens on high.
Guanyin sits upon the Pāṇḍava Rock, manifesting compassion; from the tips of the willow branches, jade dew drips down. How many sentient beings are submerged in suffering!
The ocean. When will the sensory dust of sound be utterly extinguished?
Sending off Chan Master Tong to Yongjia—the Buddha is not far from man—one realizes it through one's own mind.
Looking ten thousand *li* toward Yachou, an arrow pierces the shadow of the red sun; the night-light.

Radiating light, it illuminates both existence and non-existence. The monkey struck and shattered the mirror of Xuanyuan. When Yongjia arrived at Caoxi, he transmitted the mind-seal after staying for but one night.
How many people are there who enter the sea only to count its sands? They fail to distinguish the shadow of the whip from the actual horse; they cannot tell the false from the true.

I have heard that in ancient Dong’ou, the people were also flourishing. Among those who dwelt upon the mountains, their reputation was truly matched by their substance. They had no attachment to Yangqi.
Baiyun bitterly reviled Yunmen and Zhenjing; since right and wrong cannot be distinguished, gain and loss arise from the true nature.
The river moon and pine wind enter the cold of the sitting hall—awaken me from my nāga-samādhi!
Presented to the Venerable Librarian:
Huangbo’s sixty blows upon Linji were like a light reed; they revealed the profound essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as clearly as the brilliant sun suspended in the azure sky.
Waves surged and seas overflowed as Mount Taihua split apart; his swift wit and heroic eloquence thundered like a clap of lightning. I—
Why do you labor so hard to seek it out? Those who study Buddhism among the non-Buddhists rely merely on their cleverness. I ask you to let go from the very beginning and look:
every single aspect of one's own nature is inherently true.
When the Chan practitioner Songchi visited Jingshan for his second audience, he saw once and never saw again;
he heard once and never heard again. This is the conduct of a patch-robed monk:
beneath the feet of the Vajra, Mount Kunlun stands; the true body is majestic and manifest, casually cutting off heaven and earth. When Yongjia arrived at Cao...
Xi: One night spent with Zhen Dungen; nine visits to Xuefeng and Dongshan—what need is there to discuss them? A hundred turns, a thousand layers—it is simply this very thing.
It does not hinder one from helping to lift up the broken sand-bowl.
Xuan the attendant made his second visit to Jingshan;
Baizhang made his second visit to Mazu. Xuan returned once more to Jingshan. Having already arrived within the Han-yuan Palace, why seek Chang’an any further?
To say there is no Chan to be taught—this story has already spread throughout the world. It is the single transmission of Shaoshi.
Direct pointing: How could there ever have been so much as a hair’s breadth of deception? Fragrance wafts from the cassia trees by the cliffside; the wind stirs the jade-like bamboo before the eaves.
Red dust at the bottom of the well obscures the white sun; the black-spotted cat has its face covered in stripes.

As I see that the Abbot Zizang is departing for Jiangxi to pay homage to his ancestors, nine summers have not yet passed since he first resolved to travel the mountains. Why should I be in such a hurry? I shall first write a verse to see him off.
The Patriarch did not come from the West; his spiritual traces pervade the human world. If the eye at the crown of your head has not yet opened, by what means can you perceive the ultimate truth?
Beneath the feet of every person, there is a momentum that pierces the heavens. When a single thought suddenly clears into emptiness, it is as bright as the radiant sun in the sky.
The value of perfect fusion lies in entering the subtle; its liveliness and freedom reside in fierce intensity.

Like stars flying across a mirror’s surface, like lightning rolling away the film from one’s eyes—when applying the function before the pivot of the mechanism, when wielding the staff to humble Deshan or letting out a shout to surpass Linji, how could there ever have been any fixed limits or measures?
Releasing and gathering, in every instance one transcends; therefore, in daily life, do not stitch things together with substantial dharmas.
To swallow the Western River in a single gulp is to accord with the truth even before a word is raised.
Sending off Master Mingzang to Jiangxi and Jiangnan:
he goes directly like this. When pressed, he does not come; his entire body is mud and water. He stands before the sun, moon, and devas;
he dwells atop the towering, precipitous Wondrous Peak. This is a lion cub of the West River—*tshao-chao*! (A roar! He emerges!
A turning-phrase from within the cave: cast aside Yunmen’s “the six do not contain it. From the tip of the staff, the entire universe stands forth alone and exposed.
—Composed for the departure of Vinaya Master Sheng on a journey to Jinling.
At dawn, we bid farewell as we travel to Mount Zhongfu. Where could there be a single word to offer?
It is most excellent, clearly manifest at the tips of the hundred grasses, its brilliant radiance outshining the stars and constellations. The ancients said it was not a matter of the tongue;

when meeting, one should speak of it frequently. Cast off the head-stall, unload the pack-saddle; how could one fall into the tracks of the paths of sages or ordinary folk? Thus it was in antiquity, and so it is today.
You must look for yourself: the green mountains wind and turn like coiling dragons and snakes. Selling away one’s single robe is but an ordinary matter;
one need not fear the frost-wind that pierces to the bone.
—Sent to Chan Master Zhao.
Whether the Way is attained or not, it is the root and stem of the myriad dharmas. Illumination and function are simultaneous;

when the great void gives rise to a cataract, the eighty-four thousand *vinaya* rules and the three hundred and sixty dharma assemblies form a layered, interlaced net of Indra, each and every one of them harmoniously integrated and sovereign.
The principle is like the point of an arrow; the phenomenon exists like a lid fitting its box. Following the teachings, jade turns and pearls revolve, never opposing the various sensory dusts.
The diamond sword is best held at the side; the black-lacquered bamboo whisk divides front and back.
How high is heaven? How thick is earth? In the vastness of heaven and earth, who knows? To the south of the Xiang and north of the Tan, the bamboo grows in the south and the... in the north.
Dì Mù: This practice is upright and capable of continuing the fundamental lineage. As the five branches of the school join in their fragrant blossoming, behold these lofty footsteps.
Sending off Chief Seat Yuē:
Last night the west wind arose amidst the forest trees; this morning we part from a man of high character. I only entreat you to do good on your journey.
Having met, there is a glimpse for those who understand; how much more so when the Dharma is preached from the celestial palace? A single stroke of the mind is like a flash of lightning;
transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations, it surpasses both two, three, four, and seven.
Who cares about the winnowing basket of Jiangxi? It even makes one choke on the water while drinking.
Seeing off Chief Seat Ding as he returns to the deep mountains of Xichuan and the bitter waters of Shu: going and staying are fundamentally without fixed mind; look at the path beneath your feet.

With eight facets of brilliance and a spirit like a rainbow, standing like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high, he swallows Buddhas and patriarchs. Universal Worthy is not on Mount Emei; how could Mañjuśrī ever come?
In the eastern land, as the majestic elephant carriage advances along the rugged path, the lion turns back with a lowing roar.
Beneath the layered canopy of the Celestial Palace, the patrons and the administrators of the monastery witness the manifestation of auspicious relics.
Before the peaks of Mount E, within the Hall of the Sun-King, the clay niches and plastered statues stand out starkly against the void, weathered by the sun’s heat and the wind’s blow.
Ah! Adorned with a hundred blessings; towering with ten thousand phenomena are the thirty-two marks. Deshan broke it off so nothing remained; Danxia burned it into a firebrand.
Since such vigor is utterly absent, what need is there to speak of making offerings of the True Dharma?
Covering it from the beginning, in the end he returns it to its measureless state. Those who hold up their fists hold up their fists; those who join their palms join their palms.
Those who rejoice, rejoice; those who praise, praise. This single assembly on Mount Lingyan remains solemnly as if it had not yet dispersed.
Yangqi’s diamond circle and Shichuang’s leaking oil lamp shatter the pearl within the Tathāgatagarbha; how could there be any limit to the beings of the human and celestial realms thus awakened?
Following the rhyme of Master Dongzhou of Huqiu, I send off a monk returning to Sichuan:
