A man of great capacity cannot lift his feet; yet he raises his stride and traverses the journey. Turning his head, he loses sight of his own self. With a single move, the wondrous wheel of the pivot turns;
in the blink of an eye, he has traveled three thousand li. In vain do you speak of the wind-chasing heavenly horse galloping away; it is all for naught.
He proclaims that the fierce dragons of the sea are at play; when the arrow is fixed upon the string, a single shaft pierces three barriers.

As a mustard seed is cast into a needle’s eye, a thousand differences are simultaneously resolved. Having swept past the Qutang and Yanwu rapids, the golden circle and the thorny bramble are but mundane accoutrements.
To Zhuncang Abbot of Huqiu: People do not recognize the mani-jewel;
When one obtains it, its utility is truly extraordinary. I say that within the Tathāgatagarbha there is none;
Yet sometimes it is sought within one's robes. Chan Master Zhun has found a basketful; He has emptied it all, scattering it toward Yunyan.
The Old One smelts and shatters empty space into two sides; the four sevens and two threes all fall over together. Priceless, yet there is room for discussion;
having set aside Mount Sumeru, there is nowhere to seek it. Parting the weeds and observing the wind to test the master—throughout Jiangnan and Jiangbei, they are as numerous as rice and hemp.

Accompanied by the Head Seat Lín and other practitioners, I have come to Qinchuan. The waters of the Qin are so clear they can be scooped up; I shall take a single scoop of this purity to douse the poison of affliction.
With twin talismans suspended from his elbow and a third eye set upon his brow, he occupies the seat in Huiri Hall; demons and heretics dare not approach him.
I possess a lute of scorched *tóng* wood; its strings have long been broken and not yet mended. Master Mǎ once played it for me, yet Old Páng could not hear enough.
Alas! These eighty men, each one of them rolling like a wheel—were it not for this slight contest, how could this melody have been heard?

As the *udumbara* flower blooms once more for Attendant Jiu’s second visit to Master Tiandong, one may smell it, yet no fragrance is found. If one is a true man of the Way, they will certainly know its place of origin.
Movement and stillness immediately diverge; deliberation results in artifice and hypocrisy. Having sat and severed the barrier at the very summit, every step transcends words and meaning.

Attendant Jiu of Yingjiang possessed a lofty spirit in both his public life and seclusion. He had extensively studied under various masters of the ancestral way, and his character was remarkably extraordinary.
He is like the Eight Divine Horses, leaping thirty thousand li in a single bound. I thus recall Old Xizhou, whose radiance illuminates heaven and earth;

he bore the lineage of the Dongshan school and upheld the intent of the Western Patriarch. Through the principle of mutual interpenetration, he established the correct and the pervasive, never transgressing the boundaries of the five ranks.
In days past I ascended his hall; this journey now brings me back again. The coral is shattered and the bright moon-jewel broken;
the phoenix no longer dwells upon the wutong tree.
In the same rhyme, two stanzas presented to Imperial Censor Lian.

Loyal and righteous conduct has been passed down through generations; your pure reputation reaches the celestial capital. You hope to bring salvation to the people and all things, relying on your strength to uphold the fundamental principles.

Your embroidered robes shine with brilliance, and your sweet rain moistens the parched and withered. Your practice of the Way rivals that of the ancient sages, and your governance is a far-reaching plan.
Eating moss, I am but a humble rustic; my woodpeckers' beaks wear away, yet I am no mere firewood-gatherer. The Buddha’s prophecy is truly difficult to forget;
how could I fail to repay the Imperial Grace? My loyal heart shall never grow old; may I join those who offer the "Flower Prayer" and the "Song of Mount Song."

Once wielding the jade axe, he roamed the ends of the earth; Heeding the decayed and eliminating the treacherous, he never erred. A pure wind from the halls and towers chilled both court and countryside;
In his laughter and talk, he occasionally granted admittance to the ranks of monks.
In the same rhyme, I send off the Elder Jin of Goryeo as he returns to the capital:
A man of the Way came from Goryeo to visit me amidst the mountains and waters; His resolve was sharp and unwavering, for he hoped to cause the teachings to circulate.

The Mother shall leave behind two distant traces; it is necessary to follow after Huili and Huisong. In years to come, when ten thousand fingers circle around you, you will exhaust your strength to spur on the elephant and the dragon.

Your divine mechanism of wondrous appearance and disappearance makes even Buddhas and Patriarchs find their tracks difficult to trace. When the ten thousand assemblies gather at the Heavenly Capital, how could one still distinguish between west and east?
Like the king of all valleys, to which the Yangtze and Han rivers both flow as their ultimate destination, so it is with my Way; how could its exposition ever be exhausted?
It is like a clear, still pool in a white jade pond, or a towering palace of blue lotuses. Seated upon this dais of a hundred jewels, you stand out preeminent like Mount Kongtong.

The Emperor’s countenance is but a few inches from my gaze; his voice resonates like a great bell. He sits upright as the North Star, while I offer high prayers for the pines of the Southern Mountain.

May the Buddha-sun illuminate the dark alleys, and may the spring breeze return to the garden of awakening. When your task is accomplished, you shall depart; your saffron robes will shimmer with scattered brilliance.
A Memorial for Secretary Yuzhu Buhua: Yuzhu Buhua was truly a son of the Buddha;
His self-sacrifice in seeking a verse was entirely like this. He prostrated himself before the bhikṣu-saṃgha;
In a single word of ultimate truth, he forgot both self and other. Within the three realms there is no home—who is one’s kin? The great trichiliocosm, when gathered together, is but—

A single mote of dust; within that single mote of dust, one realizes the Dharma-realm. When the youth Sudhana came to seek the Way in the south, he gave a single snap of his fingers before Maitreya’s gate.
Amidst the towering palatial towers within a world-system as small as a mote of dust, a jade pillar stands beside them, unadorned by flowers.
Together they realize the Tathāgata’s primary truth. I observe that this meaning is also not substantial; this is the power of "unflowering" diligence. From the past...
All skillful arts are utterly forgotten; at once they are yielded to Vimalakīrti. How great is the Buddha-dharma—how it must be examined with care!
Abandon what is deficient and follow what is superior. Such wondrous applications of supernatural power are but secondary matters; when all myriad activities have ceased, one reaches the Bodhimanda.
Sending off the First *Vina* to return to his hometown to practice Zen:
one must recognize the original capacity. This teaching has been unknown by anyone, past or present. The golden crow merely senses it passing overhead;
in the midst of turmoil, how can one forget their exhaustion? For a man of great character, the mind is the ancestral source prior to heaven; the true wind of Jibei (Linji) should be followed.
Carrying the burden: When Xinghua struck Kebin in those days, was there not a transmission at the tip of his staff? In the high autumn when the trees have fallen, a single peak is cold;
with an iron staff slung over his shoulder, he departs from Changgan. Having beheld the face of the Venerable Jueluo at the waterfall, he meets you now with a joyful countenance.
Who could have said that over five thousand scrolls were sent to the Librarian [Mu*Ji]?
Even the Yellow-Faced Old Man had not yet reached the end. These leaves used to stop a child’s crying must be picked up once more;
remove the specks of dust from the eyes of those who are but children. This man of the Way is naturally a "thousand-li colt"—as he travels along, how could he ever forget?
Racing and galloping—cutting off the myriad streams in a single phrase. A hundred-bushel, radiant *maṇi* jewel. Old Xiujū merely draws back in dismay.
"Ask me: on what day will you come again? The sound of pines at the eaves of the house proclaims it for him.
Do not pick up the staff by the bedside—*Du!* (A rebuke!)
Imitating the "Poem on Xin-feng" to See off the Zen Practitioner Fu:
In early autumn and late summer, one goes east and west. The three realms are vast and boundless; where can one dwell? Companions on the Way pass each other shoulder to shoulder.

The staff resting upon the shoulder is the phrase that pervades the whole body. The moon sets over the long sky as the waters of a thousand rivers flow; Ten thousand trees are startled by the wind, their leaves falling.
The first fall: face-to-face presentation, falling into the precipice; cast behind one’s back, yet right before one’s eyes it is denied.

Suddenly crying out, "What does the Golden-Haired One fear?"—a single roar startles heaven and earth. His tracks leave him nowhere to be found; he reveals the meaning of the Patriarch who came from the West.
Spreading his mat, he sells it for three thousand miles; for what purpose did he undergo such hardship in those days? Parting from me...
Descending from Fengtai in the Ming Dynasty, do not forget your original vow to travel in search of the Dharma.
To the physiognomist Zou Tianran of Jiangxi, who is also observing geomancy:
in examining people, one must examine the mind; in observing the earth, one must observe the principle. One should know that this principle and the mind are neither one nor two.
Investigating the source of the myriad dharmas, one must return to the root to grasp the essential meaning. This allows one not only to know others, but also to recognize oneself.
What glory is there in wealth and honor? What shame is there in poverty and low station? Therefore, for those who dwell in the mountains and forests, their joy surpasses that of the capital markets.
Naturally in accord with the words of wisdom: to know the words is to know where to rest.
As the Abbot Zangzhu departs for the East, the jade key in his hand weighs a thousand *qun*; the halo behind his head extends ten thousand *zhang*. He turns toward the Tathāgata-garbha.
Look! When you reach home, you must surely act to propagate [the Dharma].
The spring at Fengtai in Jinling has already faded; it is fitting to return southward from ten thousand *li* as soon as possible. Within the Great Tang Empire there is no Zen master;
when engaging in question and answer with such freedom, do not be hasty. To say that it exists is still delusion; how can this school be discussed?

East and west, appearing and disappearing according to the occasion like swift lightning; great function, bestowing and taking away like crashing thunder. I now have no words, so you should cease your inquiry;
yet mindful of your earnestness and repeated requests, I take up my brush by the bright window and write this long song.
Outside the window, the plum blossoms cast their clear shadows.
I, Shi, once witnessed this profound statement. Previously, after he had merely transcribed the first four lines, he proceeded to write down the location as "the Phoenix Terrace in Jinling.
When he was about to write his own name, [the Master] stopped him. Shi then covered [the writing area] with his hand and said:
"I beg you to compose a long song for me. Thereupon, the old man wrote the three characters "Spring has already passed" (*chūnyǐlǎo*).
He then appended the four characters "Jīnlíng Fèngtái" to form the line, thus completing the long song. Furthermore, in the *Bǎoníng Lù*, he instructed the attendant:
There was one whose sincere heart was like iron or stone, and who possessed the verse, "Only in years to come shall he be fit to be a son of my house";
he was this very man. Formerly his style name was Bieyuan; it is not known how he is now.
As the Daoist master Baozang departs for Fusang, the sun is at its zenith. Beneath his feet there are no waves; before his eyes, Buddhas and patriarchs are empty.
Within the five thousand and forty-eight volumes of the Tripitaka lies the divine pearl; throughout the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates, the thicket of entanglements is spread.
Sweeping away the golden rooster and brushing aside the jade hare, with a chilling breath that could cut through hair, he utters a "Duo! and draws a glance.

This startles old Shaoyang, leaving him with no way to evade; Chan Master Muzhou spent his life carrying a wooden board, while old Xuefeng lost one of his eyes. The lineage’s style has fallen to the ground.
It is also difficult to support with one's hands. In withered trees and cold crags, the springtime can be summoned;

yet when a tiger roars from the forest and a python hisses across the ridge, the mastery of killing and giving life lies entirely with the person themselves. Within the boundless realm of the Great Tang, north, south, east, and west are but a single body.
Master Dongzhou sent me a verse concerning his lost teeth; I respond with four verses in the same rhyme. The teeth have fallen out, yet the meaning grows deeper;
Having silenced the throat, the wondrous sound is emitted. To the very bottom, it has nothing to do with lips or tongue;
In the end, it is entirely the heart of the Patriarch. There are no secret words to be transmitted or bestowed; There is only the true standard that may be followed.
The power and responsibility: weeds fill the Dharma Hall to a height of ten feet;

indeed, there is no path for others to seek. When [the Master] raises it up facing the sun, how profound is his intent! It is all the sound of the *huángzhōng* and *dàlǚ* tones. Knocking and clashing against teeth and gums, there is truly a source;
contending at the lips and mouth, he is fundamentally without artifice. A tiger with wings sprouting from its shoulders—people naturally fear it; who can pluck the pearl from the dragon’s chin?
It is fit for use; the "Wind of the Sleeping Tiger Gate" is exactly like this.
It spares the Zen monks from forced searching; they dwell most deeply in bamboo huts and thatched halls. They are frequently startled by the reports of their fellow practitioners arriving.

Not using seductive charms to buy fame in the age, he simply uses his guidance to serve the hearts of the multitude. Let the dull-natured steed rest at the manger; cutting across the stream is still the work of the elephant.
The King’s appointment: before his gate, a hundred birds come and go; take care not to be caught by the hunter.

When attained, it is refined and subtle; when applied, it is profound. Sitting grandly in the light of the sun, he manifests the mysterious sound. Under the blue sky and bright sun, the words of the fundamental principle—the ancient Buddha-mind within the lamp-stand and the oil-canister.
Boarding the boat of the sea of suffering, one will surely reach the shore; curing the ailment of the incurable, it is truly effective.
Capable and fit; upon the crown of his head is a single eye of Maheśvara. Though blind, he cannot be sought by those who are merely sighted.

Presented to Master Chuangmen, following the rhyme of the High Monk from Beyond the Lakes, whose Way and resonance are extraordinary: facing each other on the night bed, we are both filled with joy. The poem is composed—jade turning and pearls returning.
A decade has passed; it comforts me in these times when heaven seems desolate and earth grown old. It is better to leave no trace or shadow behind at all.
Let us all tear down the old藩篱 (fānlí—barrier/fence). Reflecting on this, I think of Puhua’s profound compassion; Linji once called him a "little servant boy."
Layman Chen, carrying the verses of various mountain masters, traveled to visit the Abbot Jian and received them (in the rhyme of Master Dongzhou of Huqiu):
"North of the Wuxiang Bridge lies the home of water and clouds; Ordinary and holy beings pass through like rice and hemp.
Since we cook equal 'rice-less' meals, We must diligently serve the tea that tests men. The Patriarchal Masters have shown us how to begin; The Elder shall bring it to completion."
In an instant, with a single snap of the fingers, one ascends to the realm of Gandhavyūha. A great rain of sweet nectar waters the sprouts upon the fiery mountain.

Entrusted to a fellow practitioner at Nanping, the reputation spreads far enough to fill a carriage. The bowl and staff are deeply entrusted to the House of Dharma; may they exhaust the waters by the shores of Lake Xi Zi.
Water. It quenches the thirst that kills the "Tortoise-Nose" snake of the Southern Mountain. Were it not for the pearl of the Dragon King’s palace, there would surely be flaws;
as for the jade of the Lián-chéng, it is certainly without blemish. I laugh at how many who vie for supremacy merely boast of their own worn-out mechanisms.
Seeing off Chan Practitioner Yi as he returns to the Lion’s Den in Siming:
The cub’s claws and fangs are already as sharp as needles. From now on, he shall traverse the Three Rivers and Nine Dams;
All manner of monsters and demons shall be utterly banished. With a shout, he sweeps the white clouds and seizes the Jade Hare; He cleaves open the blue seas and leaps across them.
Whale! Father, your two eyes hang like the red sun; I look for you to return and stroke the tiger’s whiskers.
To a friend:

when matters reach the heart, it is easy to fall into sorrow. Seeing our former companions as the morning stars and waning moon, let us speak of our feelings and act as those who have entered the cage together.
The bird dreams of sharing its cage with the monkey; Baizhang once again took refuge with Mazu. What was Shuangfeng’s intention in receiving Niutou?
Let us all rise together for the *santai* dance; it is simply to let people laugh and then leave it at that.
I heard from Elder Yongxi that the surging river waves can overturn a boat; yet on this journey, I am fortunate that the current is calm. Meeting you today comforts me of my ten-year dream;
what prevents us from parting our canopies for three days? I have no pack-cloths or straw hats to burden my person; there are only clouds and mountains as my companions.
A superior journey. Ashamed that his sense of shame did not follow Elder Fu, he lets the cold horns rise upon the city towers.
The boat for sending Officiant Chao to Jiangxi to pay homage to the Patriarchs has been purchased for many days already;
yet the verse is still not finished—how can this be? Who is it whose lineage is distinct and whose eyes are extraordinary?

Matters: Piercing the weeds and observing the wind—how could this belong to another? Traveling ten thousand *li* south, the whale-waves were perilous; ascending the western mountains with a single staff, the peaks of Chu were many.
The ancestral masters’ sacred bones have all turned to dust; at the tips of the myriad blades of grass, ants build their nests.
In the style of Master Hezhong’s “Verses on the Mountain Dwelling of Puna,” I write:

The livelihood of a man of the Way lies within a mountain cleft. Who would say that the affairs within a mountain cleft are more numerous? He brushes aside the myriad phenomena to open up the ultimate azure void;
He chews upon emptiness until the Yellow River is exhausted. At the edge of his verse, he requires no divine assistance; Upon his crown, let the magpies do as they please.
A nest is built; the profound barriers of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are all shattered. When guests enter the room, do not brandish your halberds.

I bid farewell to the Abbot Jing of Xixian, who carries his head high and wears horns as he descends from Long Peak. Amidst ten thousand ravines beneath the clouds of the Five Elders, the precious treasury is flung open and the pearls are revealed.
It turns; a torrential spring gushes forth from the cavernous rock. If you have not yet forgotten the clinging to dharmas, do not claim to understand;
only when the dust of emotional afflictions is entirely extinguished will you see the true merit. Luopo never studied under Jiaqiao; the pickle jar of one house is shared by a hundred.
Sending off Secretary Yue on his return to the East:
Water lies deep in the mountain stream, the moon is in the sky. The Patriarch extracted the mystery within the phrase.
Tomorrow, ten thousand miles beyond the Long River, he will sweep past Fusang and even further than that.
Inscription on the Wall Paintings of Landscape by the Censor Sītòu The Censor’s mind dwells amidst hills and ravines;
Sītòu’s brush brings forth wind and rain. An old monk sits here in this Hall of Ice and Snow;
From the treetops, the heavenly flowers fall with a whistling sound.
The stele for Master Dingshan, requested by Ba Jianfu, contains verses on his travels and a record of his virtue, conduct, and righteousness that move people’s hearts;
it is like a magnet meeting a needle—it happens spontaneously, without waiting for anything else.
Master Dingshan dwelt in deep seclusion in the Western Mountains. His solitary style and brilliant integrity were like the light of the stars or the radiance of the moon;

there was no one who did not look up to him with reverence. When the seat at Donghu became vacant, his friends from the rivers and lakes joined their voices in harmony to offer a *gāthā* in his praise.
This so-called expression of feeling through words upon hearing the news—was this truly because the old man required such external stimulus? Long ago, [it was said of] Fén...
When Yang did not emerge to serve as a man, Chan Master Cong opened the door and roused him; the Linji school’s spiritual influence relied upon his support and cultivation.
To view this scroll once again is like looking back at the past from the present: how could one consider sleeping peacefully to be a sound strategy?
The verses and sayings of Venerable Wuzu bore the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
they penetrated to the very source of the Dharma, and his eloquence was unimpeded like a pearl rolling upon a tray.
Only then can one be said to be able to cure the fatal illness of humanity. Now, observing this scroll, it is evident that when he spread the paper and wielded the brush—
It is like wind blowing across the surface of water, naturally forming ripples; how could there be any intentional effort in its arrangement?
The Dharma-gate of Dongshan unfolds right view with such brilliance that it is as manifest as the sun in a clear blue sky. I say that the venerable Yuanzhao attained this.
Three days after the recorded sayings of the Senior Seat-holder Bajiao were finished, I did not see him again;
he was no longer the same as before. Master Jiao, the Librarian, visited me in the third month of this year and departed quickly;
yet within less than half a year, what he has attained far surpasses his former state. This record is the profound realization of a true practitioner of the Way.
This is indeed the duty of one who has attained true awakening. At another time, while circulating the ancestral Way, he was able to rouse the scholars from their chronic illness at the vital points;
of this, there can be no further doubt.
Master Zhu Tian of Ba Yuan Tong, known as Old Dongshan, said to Nantang:
"Although I have inherited the lineage of Master Baiyun Chuan, I habitually employ the methods of Master Yuanluo to receive disciples.
This is because Baiyun’s speech was crude and could not be taken as a model. I say that Baiyun was indeed crude.
Even the site of Old Dongshan is difficult to reach, let alone that of Nantang. Master Zhutian of Yuan Tong received the Dharma from the late Nanshan Fuxin Huizhao Chan Master.
Having observed the wondrous function of Fuxin’s pedagogical devices, he spoke with utter spontaneity and attained realization with total freedom of mind.
Yet, when it came to matters of rigorous severity and meticulous detail, he possessed the style of the ancient masters of our school. How could this be...?

Are you not also one who is clumsy at tilling the fields of Indian [Buddhism]? Your *Recorded Sayings* from the four assemblies are like a swift horse on a common road, galloping so far as to leave the dust behind, outstripping the sun and chasing the wind, covering a thousand li in an instant.
Even if Master Dongshan were to be reborn in his old age, he would surely fold his hands in reverence. How profound is the saying:
"The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs can only be transmitted when the disciple's wisdom surpasses that of the teacher. Indeed!
Regarding the *Recorded Sayings* of Master Bahui Ji:
The elder Master Huiweng moved from Baiyang to Nanping, from Nanping to Shuangjing, and from Shuangjing came to Dayang.
Although this record did not exist at that time, it was already known that he was a master who possessed the Way. His great voice resounded like a crashing gong.
The Way of Linji, which revives the Buddhas and Patriarchs—how flourishing it is! You, Attendant, should preserve it firmly.
*The Collected Lost Verses and Eulogies of Master Gulin*, Volume Lower (End).
The Life of Master Gulin.
The Master’s name was Qingmao; his courtesy name was Gulin; he styled himself Jingangdang, and in his later years was called Xiujusou. He was the son of the Lin family of Leqing, Wenzhou.

His paternal ancestors had followed the Confucian profession for generations. His mother, Lady Xue, served the Buddha with the utmost devotion. She gave birth to three sons, of whom the Master was the youngest.
On the night of his conception, she dreamed of the Great Being Śākyamuni (Sengqie Dashi), who presented her with a blue lotus flower and said: "Congratulations..."
"You shall have a son who will become the eye of the world. She then scattered various flowers over him. Upon waking, he felt an extraordinary sense of clarity and refreshment.

He was born on the first day of the eighth month in the *Renxu* year of the Jingding era of the Song dynasty (1262). Before reaching his third birthday, whenever he saw people, he would immediately join his palms and smile.
At the age of ten, he recited the Lotus Sūtra with his peers from the village shrine. Upon reaching the chapter on King Wonderful Adornment, he was moved to tears by its profound meaning.

He petitioned his parents to allow him to leave the household life, but they would not permit it. Consequently, he abandoned sleep and food. The following year, his maternal uncle returned from Hangzhou, and he took him as his teacher.
He thought to himself, "This heavenly being has taken pity on me. He petitioned his mother with even greater urgency; she took compassion on him and informed his father.
His father said, "Leaving the household life is no small matter. I feared there would be none who could fulfill his resolve. Now that your maternal uncle has arrived, it is precisely the right time.
Although his kinsmen all tried to restrain him, they could not prevail. Thereupon, he followed his uncle westward. The following year, he returned to Tiantai and relied upon the State Preceptor.
In the year following [his ordination], Master Qing Guyan received full ordination. One day, as the Master ascended the hall, he cited the words of Master Gao’an Wuzu:

"Whenever a monk enters the room for private instruction and does not immediately accord with the teaching, I examine his arm and say: 'Your parents gave you this body; your friends have helped you realize your aspirations.
You are free from the pressure of hunger and cold, and free from the toil of conscription and labor. At such a time, if you do not remain steadfast—'"
"If you do not exert firm diligence and accomplish the work of the Way, what face will you have when you see your parents, teachers, and friends on that day?

When the Master heard this, his tears fell in profusion. Therefore, he later often said: "At that moment, I knew there was a way to transcend birth and death and repay the profound kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Not long after, the Yuan dynasty underwent a revolution and the great army pressed upon the borders. There was a soldier who...

When a blade was placed against the master’s neck, he did not change his expression. Once the matter was settled, he traveled extensively to seek instruction, first visiting Chan Master Jianweng Jing at Xuedou.
After Jing passed away, those who succeeded him wished to invite the master, but he immediately fled; everyone held him in high esteem.
At that time, his reputation spread far and wide. He subsequently went to see Chan Master Gong at Nanping Shilin.
Upon seeing him, Gong said, "Although this youth is but a junior, he is indeed fit for refinement. He then asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "Wenzhou.
Shilin said, "When Yongjia reached Caoxi, why did he lose his nostrils? The Master was speechless. After a short while, he presented a verse, saying: "Yongjia reached Caoxi; [The verse continues...]"
"How could the nostrils ever be lost? Shaking his mendicant’s staff, he circles the meditation platform. 'Nine times nine is eighty-one.
Yunlin said, "This is indeed excellent, yet I fear you have misunderstood it. Try explaining it to me. As the Master was about to open his mouth, Yunlin shouted, "As expected, you have misunderstood!
The following day, Yunlin ascended the hall and presented this to the assembly, speaking with stern exhortation. The Master was indignant and felt unjustly treated. Once—

He returned to the hall and did not step outside its gates, vowing to achieve thorough realization. After two months of entering the master’s room for instruction, he heard the master cite the dialogue concerning the *shu* bamboo shoots of the Southern Mountains and the black beetles of the Eastern Sea;
at this, he attained a slight awakening. Upon the passing of Master Lin, the teacher went to Chengtian Temple in Suzhou to see Chan Master Jue’an Zhen, with whom he conversed.
Zhen remarked to others, "This is a person who has come back again. From this point on, his reputation spread among his peers.
At that time, Xiaodamo was serving as the *fàngmùliáo* (pasture attendant) at Nengren Monastery in Yandang under Zen Master Hengchuan Hongguang, who had retired from his official duties.

Hongguang severely criticized the teachings and proclamations of various quarters, asserting that they were all merely flowery rhetoric suited to the times, which caused the True Dharma to degenerate into mere sophistry.
Although Hongguang had retired from his post, he remained tireless in exhorting and inspiring others. Upon hearing of this reputation, Xiaodamo traveled with double speed to pay his respects.
Zhaozhou also knew the Master’s reputation beforehand. When he arrived, it was three days before he was permitted to meet him;

yet, without exchanging a single word, Zhaozhou realized that ten-eighths of what he held dear in his heart had already vanished. He then remained as a disciple. Later, when Zhaozhou brought out a massive volume of his own lifelong writings, Zhaozhou ultimately burned them, saying:
"The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not a matter of mere talent or eloquence; it must necessarily transcend emotional consciousness and proceed directly."

"Exhausting the root and source, one must die and then be revived again before being fit for refinement. Only then will you be able to hold the handle of the ladle for others in the future, so as not to lead people’s sons and daughters astray;
otherwise, you are not of our lineage. The Master was suddenly struck with a flush of heat and broke into a sweat.
From that moment on, his body and mind were instantly stilled, becoming as withered and parched as dead wood. One day, Chuang looked at the Master and said, "A monk asked Yunmen: 'Not...'"
"Is there still a fault in giving rise to even a single thought? Yunmen replied, "Mount Sumeru. Before the sound of these words had faded, the Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment.
He cried out in a stern voice, "The Old Monk is ruining people's sons and daughters! Yunmen grabbed him and said, "Where did you see Yunmen?
The Master pushed him away and said, "When Mr. Zhang drinks wine, Mr. Li gets drunk," and then prostrated himself. Yunmen gave him a blow.
*Tà*. From this point on, their spiritual resonance was mutually attuned, and his realization grew deeper by the day.

At the age of nineteen, the following year he returned to Guoqing Temple and composed three hundred poems modeled after those of Hanshan. Thus, there is a later verse titled "Seeing off a Monk Returning to Tiantai":

"Throughout his life, he has been too indolent to open his mouth; Now, with a 'duò duò,' he attempts to compose three hundred verses. Who can truly know the definitive true sound? It is as it was in antiquity."

Regarding the phrase "neither before nor after now," when Ryōkai arrived at Yokawa to reside at Yūō-ji in response to the imperial summons, the master Soku, the chief storekeeper of Eizan, came to him.
Before long, he returned to the Zakubō quarters. Having long attended upon eminent masters, he had already established himself as one who stood in the shadow of their excellence.
At that time, there was one named Hō under Ryōkai’s guidance who was particularly outstanding; thus, Ryōkai would often say, "Only the two masters Hō and Shū are capable..."
Having understood where the old monk’s tongue falls, he stayed at the Yuyang Monastery for six years. He then traveled again to Gusu to visit Master Qi Chan.
On his way via Qiantang, he was invited by Master Gaofeng Yun of Mount Jing to spend the summer retreat there.

All the famous monks there were delighted by his travels and requested that the Master provide a judgment on the instructions given within the Yunmen lineage room, as well as various other karmic conditions; they questioned him accordingly, and he responded to each inquiry.
The guests in the hall were struck with astonishment. In the autumn, he arrived at Lingyan in Pingjiang, where Master Qi invited him to serve as the keeper of the treasury.

Subsequently, while at the Guimeng Hall of Chengtian, he was held in such high esteem and veneration by Master Fuyan Fu that the latter exerted great effort to persuade him to share the teaching seat.

Later, he entered the world at Baiyun Chan Temple during the Tianting era. He became the successor to this hermitage and resided there for nine years before moving to Kaiyuan, where the monastic community flourished exceedingly.
Some say that from ancient times, when talent is high, slander arises; when the Dharma prospers, demons manifest—it is not always a source of fortune.
After about half a year, he indeed encountered an unexpected disturbance and withdrew. Master Yong of Dongzhou at Huqiu cleared a room for him.
He was invited to reside at the ancestral pagoda temple of Longzu, where they served as both host and guest in turn, receiving visitors with boundless skill.
Thus, he composed the verse for Xiujū’s visit to Layunyan: "From the beginning of the year to its end, even with a swift pen, how could one not manage the myriad debts?"

At that time, there were two treasury stewards, Xuān and Jǔ, who served diligently at his side. When they requested instruction on Xuedou’s *Nian gu* (Capping Phrases on Ancient Cases), he would invariably append his own comments after each case was cited.
Xuān compiled these and circulated them in the world. Not long thereafter, he received an imperial decree to serve as the chief administrator of Kaiyuan Temple.
His Dharma light grew ever more radiant. In the winter of the following year, Lord Yang Guogong Anpu brought his reputation for the Way of the Teacher to the Imperial Court.
Emperor Ren bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Fuzong Pujue Foxing and granted him special protection. At that time, Yuan Gong, the Chief of the Inner Secretariat, served in the Hanlin Academy;
he sent a verse to the Master, saying: "The foremost branch atop Mount Yují—this old Chan monk chatters on and on."
I understand deeply. I once took an iron pestle to strike the icy bones; I myself marvel at using a dull blade to cut through honeycombs.

To have no mind beyond the Dharma still involves conceptual understanding; to have an eye within the phrase immediately gives rise to doubt. Without unfolding the *kāṣāya*, the meditation mat is secure—this is the wondrous *dhāraṇī* of Kaiyuan.
Furthermore, the following year he retired to live beneath the pines of T'ien-p'ing, later moving to Yung-fu in Ryo. His Way—
The wind blew fiercely. At that time, Master [Fengxue] took the *Zhongmen Shoushi Shu* (The Book for Sustaining the World through the School Gate) as his basis;
among the works under the *Chuan Deng Lu*, the *Zongyao* was considered the most comprehensive and systematic. Master Yong’s compilation ended with the Yuanfu era.

Subsequently, the world-renowned patriarchs provided kōans and exegeses, yet over the years these have fallen into decline. No one has yet followed Master Yong’s intent to compile and continue them. [This work begins at] Jiang [of Yongjia].

His mind was vacant and his seat empty. The officials of the monastery wished for the Master to receive the honor of a grand ceremonial procession and earnestly entreated him; however, though they sent messengers three times, he did not rise.
They then presented him with a verse, which said: "I, an old man, no longer harbor thoughts of my native land; it seems we do not belong to the same lineage within True Enlightenment."
...and so forth. Before many days had passed, an order arrived from Baoning in Jiankang. It was impossible not to depart.

The officials of the Imperial Secretariat and the Censorate feared that the Master would not rise [to accept the summons], so they specifically dispatched the eunuch-monk Sengjia Nu to gallop with an official letter of invitation, explaining the reasons why he must come.
Consequently, the assembly in Raoyang wished to detain him, but it was not permitted; they wept as they offered money, and the official boat cast off its moorings for the farewell ceremony.
Colorful canopies obscured the clouds and the sun. When he traveled south through Nankang, the various Chan masters of Mount Lu came to meet him by the water’s edge.
As he passed through places such as Chiyang and Anqing, those who sought his Dharma words received them from his swift brush; in total, there were more than a thousand sheets of paper.

Upon entering the temple and ascending the hall, he let forth a great voice that resounded once; all followed him with deep reverence, such that even the great "dragons and elephants" from all quarters could not compare.

He did not wish to serve as a menial attendant, but hoped instead to hear the most profound mysteries. Consequently, the ears and eyes of the high officials, both monastic and lay, were newly refreshed.
Before long, all neglected affairs were restored. Previously, the Abbot Miaogong had sought instruction from the Master;

at that time, while the Master was staying in the imperial court, the Abbot received special consolation and inquiries after his health. The following winter, he went to the Suzhai Terrace to sweep the ancestral stupa, whereupon the monastics and laity requested him to preach the Dharma.

On the occasion of the *Wanshou* (Ten-Thousand-Year) celebration, people from near and far, both young and old, assembled to witness and hear [the teachings], their shouts of joy thundering like rolling waves.

Furthermore, the following year, Emperor Ying bestowed an imperial edict for the Master to inquire after the Way; the provincial decree was issued twice to dispatch him from Jiankang, yet the Master cited illness and did not rise to comply.

Not long thereafter, the Court established a Great Assembly at Mount Jinshan, commanding the three eminent masters of the various schools in Zhejiang to take turns proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma. All [the officials]...

Consequently, high officials of the provincial and court governments dispatched messengers in rapid succession to prostrate themselves before his seat, making earnest requests with great ceremony.
When the Master began his formal discourse, it was like sounding the lion’s lute; the multitude was struck with awe and submission. The Master resided at Baoning for eight years. Once...

Those who had long harbored such maladies could not help but feel a sense of solemn self-reflection. In the autumn of the Ji-si year, he would often say to his students:
"I shall not remain long. You all must exert yourselves. Those who come to collect me from the prison in the eighth month, I entrust you with the message that they should return early;
we may yet meet again. The assembly was all struck with amazement. On the eleventh day of the eleventh month, he suddenly requested a list of his robes and bowl.
He then immediately sealed and inscribed them. On the thirteenth day, several monks requested Dharma talks and true eulogies. He joyfully consented to write them for them, saying: "I..."

what leisure do I have for brush and inkstone? The chief seat had thoroughly studied the monastic community (*sōlin*), so why would he need this? He ultimately did not grant it.

Jiao then gave a shout. The Master said, "I am an old monk suffering from illness; I cannot strike you," and so forth. On the twentieth day, [the record ends].
When the elder Jiang Huiri Xuechuang saw that the Master was free from ailment, he came to bid him farewell. The Master then detained him, saying, "Escort me when I am finished.
On the twenty-first day, Chan Master Tanfang Zhong of Jiangshan and Chan Master Xiaoyin Xin of Longxiang arrived once more.
They stayed with him affectionately, unable to bear the thought of parting. Upon their departure, Jiangshan said, "The Master’s Way has been in harmony with both sovereign and subject; his fame—"
"His fame resounded throughout the universe. At the juncture of departure and arrival, one must act as the master of the Dharma gate.

The Master laughed and said, "If it were not for you, I would not have heard such words. On the twenty-second day, he fell ill. The assembly of the monastery offered prayers in the Hall of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Hearing of this, the Master rebuked them, saying, "Is life something to be craved? Is death something to be avoided? I have always loathed those in various quarters whose insight into the Way is unclear."
"At the moment of death, you pray for blessings, cast lots, and seek divinations; your confusion and perversity are worse than ignorance.
You worldly folk, why do you place me among such as these? At evening, the assembly remained surrounding him without dispersing.
A laywoman named Aoniu came to inquire after his illness and said, "When a monk reaches this point, all affairs of the monastery must be completely set aside. The Master then extended his hand.
He said, "What more is there? After a short while, his attendants requested that he leave behind a verse. The Master said, "Not yet.

Another moment passed, and when paper and brush were brought forward, he immediately began to chant in a drawn-out voice: "Last night I asked Brother Tortoise; he reported that today is auspicious. Today is auspicious!
He then wrote a verse and asked, "What time is it now? They replied, "The hour of Xu (7–9 p.m.). He nodded his head and said, "The time has come."
He immediately straightened his body and folded his hands; with eyes closed, he passed away. His remains were kept in the stupa for over ten days.

On the second day of the following month, his entire body was enshrined in a tomb on the northern plain of Master Yong’s pagoda. As the funeral bier was raised, the clouds grew somber and the wind wailed with grief.
Suddenly, from the pagoda of Tianxi Temple, five-colored light radiated afar, curving down to drench the top of the stupa. At that time, Daluhuayi of Songjiang...

The myriad beings, both noble and common, gazed upon it together, their hearts filled with a mingling of sorrow and joy, exultation and grief. The sound of their voices shook the far and near. As they approached the tomb, auspicious snow fell in profusion, like a dense rain of celestial flowers (*divyapuṣpa*);
all beings were clothed in white, and as soon as the burial was completed, the sky cleared. At that time, the Holy Sovereign bestowed white gold upon him.
He inquired after the Master’s well-being. Previously, while the Emperor was still in his private residence, he had applied his mind to the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures).
He frequently visited the Master to inquire about the Way, often returning only at the fall of evening.

Whenever he printed and distributed the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* and the *Gao-wang Guanshiyin Jing*, he invariably commanded the Master to compose a preface to manifest the Buddha-mind, placing it at the head of the scripture. This occurred in the year following his accession to the throne.
When the messenger arrived, the Master had already passed away. His worldly age was sixty-eight, and his years of monastic seniority were fifty-five.

Throughout his life, the Master provided guidance and stimulated others through numerous机缘 (ji-yuan) and dialogues; these cannot be cited exhaustively here, as they are already recorded in his *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings).

I have not recorded matters repeatedly. Since I have already engaged in frequent consultations with fellow scholars and gentlemen, I have likewise omitted those matters that lack great significance, as well as those that are already so clear they are known to all and heard by everyone.

On the first day of the eighth month of the Renxu year of the Jingding era, the Chan Master was born into the Lin family at Leqing, Wenzhou.
On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of the Jisi year of the Tianli era, he passed away at Fengtai Mountain in Jinling.
As for Bao-ning Chan Temple: its coming was for a purpose; its departure was by way of a cause.
Since Bodhidharma transmitted the Way of Kāśyapa, it has reached the twenty-eighth generation as it traveled through the land of China (Zhōngguó).
The Master transmitted it from Bodhidharma, thus completing another twenty-eight generations. Yet, from the time of Bodhidharma until now, nearly a millennium has passed.

In the interim, there were those of great capacity and great function; as for their transverse and longitudinal transformations, they strengthened the lineage’s continuity to such an extent that one could not know its measure.
By the time of the later descendants, however, branches had proliferated and trivialities competed for cleverness until the tradition was nearly on the verge of collapse.

Then there was Heungch’ŏn, who disparaged ornate embellishments and earnestly demonstrated the ancient and simple style; students began to know where to turn toward him. Yet, like a solitary crane soaring against the wind, he strove alone and exerted himself to the utmost.
Companions! A great sound is a rare resonance; it is difficult for anyone to harmonize with. Yet, upon meeting Master Chan, they became like water and ice, blue and green—blending as one.

His actions emerged from heaven, and those who followed him were swept away like grass bending in the wind. He turned the carved and ornate back to simplicity and solidity, transforming the stinking and putrid into the marvelous and divine.
He broke down the barriers of the Great Square and lifted the veil of a thousand ages. Thus, the talented and eminent men of the empire clearly perceived the lineage from above.
The matter at hand is vividly and suddenly clear, like parting the clouds and mist to behold the azure sky and the bright sun.
That which has come to pass lies precisely here. Once the task is accomplished, one departs from this world.

While the Master resided among the assembly and sat within the *bodhimaṇḍa*, a single word escaped his lips and was chanted throughout the four seas. Before his words could even be committed to print, people vied with one another to...

They were transcribed and recorded; every household possessed them and stored them at home. As for their locations, people would carry them about as they traveled, regarding them no less than a precious title-deed.
Thus, even to the very ends of the earth, there is nowhere where the words of the Master do not exist. On the day the Master passed away...
Far and near, they mourned one another as if they had lost a closest relative; their faces lost all color.

Those who lectured on the Way ceased their sessions, and those who chanted the *Brahman* sounds stopped their recitations—how much more so for those who sang songs or engaged in rhythmic labor? Thus, there were thousands who shared this same resolve.
At Cold Spring Pavilion, they prostrated themselves in rows and offered tears and sacrifices; this could indeed be seen from over a thousand *li* away.

As they were about to depart for Nalanda, the light from the tall stupa and the sacred shrine intermingled, radiating in a variegated array of five colors. Ten thousand people cried out in amazement, all saying:
"As the Buddha taught, when life ends, the subtle body (*antarābhava*) remains as a legacy. This is surely its manifestation; it has a long-standing precedent."
How much more so for this stupa, which was manifested through the transformative power of a former Buddha.

When Kang Senghui, a manifestation of a later Buddha, prayed with such sincerity that auspicious signs were brought forth, it first came into existence. From that time until now, more than twelve hundred years have passed.
Yet here we meet, and marvelous portents manifest spontaneously; such rare wonders indeed! Alas, people see only that the Master first proclaimed birth and then proclaimed extinction.

No one recognized who this Master truly was. Many years after the Master’s passing, the realm of Japan (Fusang) sought his recorded sayings (*yulu*) and carved them into woodblocks to disseminate them throughout that country.
Later, there was one who wished to travel south in search of instruction; his ship was driven by the wind until it reached Goryeo.
When the man asked about the reason for his journey, [the Master] produced a massive volume containing more than two hundred of his own verses and hymns, as if he had obtained them anew.

These precious treasures were brought back. Furthermore, at other locations within the country, several hundred more—approximately three hundred stanzas in total—were obtained, none of which had previously appeared in the Master’s published collections.
The ruler and ministers of the nation, along with its eminent scholars and the assembly of monastics, joyfully contributed their funds to have them carved into woodblocks.
They were titled *The Supplement to the Verses and Hymns of National Teacher Gulin*, and they are now revered throughout distant lands and foreign regions.

His admirers were likewise so devoted. When the Master was about to be born, his mother dreamed that the Great Being Saṃgha said to her, "Congratulations on gaining a son who shall be the eye of the world.
Upon reaching adulthood and traveling to various regions, people universally referred to him as the "Little Daruma."

Could it be that this is precisely the prophecy of the twenty-eight leaves manifesting here? Upon entering the world, he was revered as a teacher for all under heaven throughout a hundred generations;
for ten thousand ages, his heart and mind have been looked up to like the Northern Dipper and Mount Tai, with people admiring him and following him.
Furthermore, let us consider this: whether in antiquity or today, those who possess within themselves the penetration of the fundamental principle and the perfection of virtue are indeed trustworthy.
To be able to cause all under heaven—whether worthy or unworthy—to find joy in and sincerely submit to [the Way] is it not difficult?
And is it not also rare? This is something even Heaven cannot achieve; how then can man do so?

As for the fact that sage rulers, worthy ministers, and elders turn their hearts toward one and look upon one with favor, bestowing generous gifts and honors—this is merely a chance encounter of a single era.
There have been many such instances throughout past and present; they are not sufficient to constitute an honor for the Master, and I shall mention them here only in brief.
The Master’s name was Qingmao; his courtesy name was Gulin; his style was Jingangdang. He also called himself the Elder Xiujushi.

While he resided at Kaiyuan Temple for a second term, he was granted the honorary title Chan Master Fuzong Pujue Foxing. Further details are contained in his biography and stupa inscription; here, too, they are omitted in general.
I have written again. Since my Master has already enlightened so many people, those who are his true successors are indeed overflowing throughout the world and beyond the seas, propagating his Way.
Even in distant lands and foreign regions such as Japan and Fusang, they are still numerous and flourishing.
